# Text Classification {#sec-classification}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** Every number on this page was measured on
@sec-bake-off's *exact* split — the same 40,000 training and 10,000 test
reviews, recovered rather than re-drawn, for reasons @sec-classification-setup
explains. The LLM comparisons in @sec-classification-llm and
@sec-classification-crossover use a stratified 2,000-document subsample of that
same test slice, with every competing model re-scored on it;
@sec-classification-llm says why, and what it costs in resolution. Data:
`fthbrmnby/turkish_product_reviews` on Hugging Face, 235,165 rows as downloaded
and 233,508 after exact-text deduplication. Software: `scikit-learn` 1.9.0, `transformers` 5.15.0, PyTorch 2.13.0,
`imbalanced-learn` 0.14.2, `scipy` 1.18.0 on Python 3.14.5; encoder training on
an Apple M-series GPU; local LLMs through `ollama` 0.24.0.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- build the strong sparse baseline before reaching for anything larger, and say
  what it costs at every label budget rather than only at the largest one;
- fine-tune an encoder and name the budget at which it starts to be worth the
  bill;
- tell the difference between a metric that moves when your model improves and
  one that does not;
- treat class imbalance as a decision-threshold problem rather than a
  data-surgery problem, and defend that with a measurement;
- test whether the number your model calls a probability actually is one, and
  repair it when it is not;
- turn a cost matrix into a threshold, and say how much that saves over
  guessing;
- decide between a fine-tuned small model and a prompted LLM on measured
  accuracy, latency and cost;
- run error analysis as a repeatable process instead of anecdote.

## The one number to beat {#sec-classification-setup}

@sec-bake-off ended with a leaderboard. Seven representations, 40,000 Turkish
product reviews, one held-out set of 10,000, and a winner: tf-idf over word
unigrams and bigrams, fed to a **class-weighted** logistic regression, at
**76.21 [macro-F1](#gloss-macro-f1){#term-macro-f1 .term-ref}**. That the
reference point is itself class-weighted matters, and
@sec-classification-imbalance will charge it for that.
This chapter's job is to find out what it takes to beat that, and what each
increment costs.

::: {#gloss-macro-f1 .column-margin .term-gloss}
**macro-F1** — compute the F1 score separately for each class, then average
without weighting. A rare class counts as much as a common one, which is exactly
why it falls apart on this corpus when accuracy does not.
[↩](#term-macro-f1){.term-back}
:::

That framing only works if the test set is *literally the same one*. A model
scored on a different 10,000 reviews is not competing with 76.21; it is
competing with a number nobody measured. So the first thing this chapter did was
rebuild @sec-bake-off's split and check it.

That turned out to be harder than expected, and the difficulty is the first
lesson.

### Recovering a split from its fingerprint

@sec-bake-off recorded its subsample as "50,000 rows, stratified, seed 42".
@sec-clustering recorded its subsample the same way. Both are true. They are
also different samples, because "stratified with seed 42" does not name a
procedure — it names a family of procedures that disagree.

The first attempt to rebuild the split drew the subsample group by group, the
way @sec-clustering does, and produced this:

```text
                             dims      acc   macroF1   negF1
target (chapter 4)        101,659    92.57     76.21   56.47
groupby.sample            100,350    92.21     74.65   53.55
```

Every headline statistic is close and every one is wrong. A reader would not
notice; 74.65 and 76.21 both round to "about 75". But the vectoriser dimension
is not a statistic, it is a *fingerprint*: 101,659 distinct surviving n-grams is
a fact about which exact documents were in the training half. Two different
50,000-row samples will not agree on it by accident.

So we tried four constructions against that fingerprint:

```text
                             dims      acc   macroF1   negF1
target                    101,659    92.57     76.21   56.47
groupby.sample            100,350    92.21     74.65   53.55
train_test_split 50k      101,659    92.57     76.21   56.47   ← exact
train_test_split + shuffle 102,221   92.26     75.20   54.63
plain sample 50k          101,539    91.68     74.40   53.36
```

One matched on all four numbers at once. @sec-bake-off drew its 50,000 with a
single stratified `train_test_split`, and every experiment below runs on that
recovered split.

::: {.column-margin}
Note the near-miss. "plain sample 50k" lands within 120 dimensions of the target
and within one accuracy point (91.68 against 92.57) — close enough that a
careless check would accept it. Be careful about *why* the match convinces, though: these are not four
independent witnesses. `dims` is a deterministic function of which documents
landed in the training half, and the three scores are three readings of one
fitted model on one test set, so they move together. The argument is not *four
agreements* but **one very sharp agreement**: 101,659 is a six-digit count two
different 50,000-row samples have no reason to share, and the near-miss row
shows the coarser statistics would not have separated them. Nor did we prove
uniqueness — we enumerated four plausible constructions and one matched exactly.
If you ever have to recover somebody's experimental setup, pick the quantity
that is most sensitive to the thing you are trying to pin down, not the quantity
you happen to have written down.
:::

The by-product was a correction to a *different* chapter. Intersecting the two
subsamples showed that @sec-clustering and @sec-bake-off share 23,819 of their
50,000 documents — 47.6%. Both are stratified, both use seed 42, both contain
exactly 46,839 positive and 3,161 negative reviews, and they are less than half
the same corpus. @sec-clustering's margin note now says so. No validator would
have caught that; only intersecting the two sets and counting would.

**And the forensics were avoidable, which is the lesson the story does not
state.** What @sec-bake-off recorded was prose — "stratified, seed 42". What it
should have recorded is the call itself and a fingerprint of the result:

``` python
train_df, test_df = train_test_split(
    df, train_size=50_000, stratify=df["label"], random_state=42)
print(hashlib.sha256(
    ",".join(map(str, sorted(train_df.index))).encode()).hexdigest()[:12])
```

Three chapters depend on that one call, and one of them drew a different sample
without anybody noticing. Print the call, print the hash, and the fingerprint
stops being a detective story.

### The split, and the slice this chapter adds

@sec-bake-off used two slices, train and test. This chapter needs three, and
the extra one is the whole reason its numbers can be trusted: somewhere to
tune thresholds that is neither what the model learned from nor what it is
finally scored on.

```text
rows as downloaded      235,165
after de-duplication    233,508   (1,657 exact duplicates)
stratified subsample     50,000   46,839 positive   3,161 negative

  train                  40,000   37,471 positive   2,529 negative
    fit                  32,000   29,977 positive   2,023 negative
    cal                   8,000    7,494 positive     506 negative
  test                   10,000    9,368 positive     632 negative
```

@sec-bake-off used `train` and `test`. This chapter splits `train` once more,
into a 32,000-document `fit` slice and an 8,000-document `cal` slice, because
three of the things it measures — a
[decision threshold](#gloss-decision-threshold){#term-decision-threshold .term-ref},
a calibration map, a cost-optimal operating point — are *fitted quantities* that
must not be fitted on test.

::: {#gloss-decision-threshold .column-margin .term-gloss}
**decision threshold** — the cut that turns a score into a label. Almost every
classifier ships with 0.5 by default, but 0.5 is a convention, not a
measurement: it is a free parameter you are supposed to choose, on held-out
data, from what the mistakes cost you.
[↩](#term-decision-threshold){.term-back}
:::

[Every threshold in this chapter is chosen on `cal` and reported on
`test`.]{.hl} One consequence to carry into every cost comparison in this
chapter: those 8,000 `cal` documents are labelled, so they are part of the
label budget. A method that needs a calibration slice costs more labels than
one that does not, and a comparison that prices only the training set is
understating it. Where a number was obtained by tuning on test, it is labelled an
**oracle** and used only as an upper bound to measure regret against.

**And every threshold is stated on the complaint side:** flag the review when
$P(\text{complaint})$ exceeds $t$. A low $t$ therefore means *catch more
complaints*. Elsewhere you will meet the other convention — the same operating
point written as 0.834 on the *satisfied* side — so when you compare notes with
somebody, establish which side you are both talking about before comparing
numbers. One convention, stated once, is worth more than any amount of care
afterwards. That
distinction does most of the work in @sec-classification-costs.

::: {.fig-cap}
The middle tier is what @sec-bake-off did not need. A model has one fitted
object — its weights. This chapter has four, and three of them are fitted
*after* training, on data the classifier never saw. Without the `cal` slice
every threshold and every calibration curve in this chapter would be reporting
on data it was tuned on.
:::
::::

::: {.column-margin}
8,000 documents is not an arbitrary size. @sec-classification-calibration fits
isotonic regression on this slice, and Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana report that
isotonic regression needs roughly a thousand calibration points before it beats
a parametric sigmoid, below which it overfits [@niculescu2005predicting]. At
8,000 — with 506 of the minority class — we are comfortably in the regime where
their result says isotonic is safe. Our own measurement agrees, which is the
only reason we say so.
:::

The baseline reproduces exactly:

```text
tf-idf 1-2 gram + LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced"),
101,659 features, 31.7 non-zeros per row

accuracy      92.57
macro-F1      76.21
complaint P   44.84    R 76.27    F1 56.47

                 predicted
              complaint  satisfied
 complaint         482        150
 satisfied         593      8,775
```

### Where this chapter ends up

Before the work, the destination. Every row below is measured later in the
chapter, and several of them came back the opposite way round from what the
literature would lead you to expect. Some of its terms (calibration error,
AUROC, a paired bootstrap) are defined only in the sections that measure them,
so read the table now for its shape and come back to it at the end.

| what we asked | what came back |
|:--|:--|
| Does fine-tuning beat 40,000 labels' worth of tf-idf? | [Yes — with 2,000 labels]{.pro} |
| Is the sparse baseline therefore obsolete? | [No. Below ~1,000 labels it wins, and it trains in 1.2 seconds]{.con} |
| Does resampling fix class imbalance? | [No. Moving one threshold matched the best of them, for free]{.con} |
| Does class weighting cost anything? | [Yes: it multiplied calibration error by 3.6×]{.con} |
| Is the model's "probability" a probability? | [Not until you fix it — and the fix is two parameters]{.con} |
| Does the textbook cost-optimal threshold work? | [Only on calibrated scores. On raw scores it overspends by up to 56%]{.con} |
| Does accuracy tell you which threshold to pick? | [No. It moved 1.3 points while recall moved 48 points]{.con} |
| Is a 7.35-point model upgrade a pure win? | [No. It fixed 332 test documents and broke 149]{.con} |
| Is the encoder uniformly better than tf-idf? | [No — it is better on long documents, 1.88× against 1.18×]{.con} |
| Are the mistakes that remain the model's fault? | [Often not. The most confident ones are label errors]{.con} |
| Does a prompted LLM ever beat a fine-tuned encoder? | [Yes — at 1,000 labels and below. At 2,000 they tie to 0.08 points]{.pro} |
| Does writing the prompt in English help? | [Only if the model is weak: +16.90 points on 3B, +0.54 on 9B]{.con} |
| Does a confidence stated in words mean anything? | [On average yes, +0.58. As a detector, AUROC 0.667 against 0.843]{.con} |
| Is the tie at 2,000 labels a real choice? | [Not once you price it. The LLM costs 142× more per document]{.con} |

: What this chapter measured {tbl-colwidths="[54,46]"}

**What we will look at.** First the number every result in the chapter is
measured against, which on this corpus is embarrassingly high before any model
exists. Then the two ways of building a classifier — a sparse baseline that is
harder to beat than it looks, and a fine-tuned encoder — and the metrics that
tell them apart, since accuracy will not. Then the part most treatments skip:
whether the number a model hands you is a probability, and how to turn it into
a decision using what an error actually costs. Finally the comparison the
chapter exists for, LLM against small model, and the two axes that settle it.

## Baselines that are hard to beat {#sec-classification-baseline}

Before adding parameters, find out what the cheap thing does *at your label
budget* rather than at the budget somebody else had. @sec-bake-off reported one
point on a curve. Here is the curve, same vectoriser, same classifier, same test
set, training on stratified subsets of `train`:

```text
labels   macro-F1   complaint-F1   features   fit time
   200      55.46          14.63        720       0.1s
   500      60.82          25.32      1,762       0.1s
 1,000      61.60          27.03      3,458       0.1s
 2,000      67.42          38.77      6,586       0.2s
 5,000      72.77          49.18     15,828       0.3s
10,000      73.44          50.87     29,149       0.4s
20,000      75.00          54.03     54,822       0.6s
40,000      76.21          56.47    101,659       1.2s
```

Three things in that table are worth more than the headline.

**The curve is still climbing at 40,000.** Going from 20,000 to 40,000 labels
bought 1.21 macro-F1 points. Doubling again would presumably buy something
similar. Nothing here has saturated, so "we used all our data" is a statement
about the budget, not about the method.

**Almost all of the gain is in the minority class.** Macro-F1 rises 20.75 points
across the whole sweep; complaint-F1 rises 41.84. The majority class was
essentially solved at 200 labels and stayed solved. [When a class is 93.7% of
your data, the average metric is mostly reporting on the other 6.3%]{.hl} —
which is exactly why @sec-bake-off used macro-F1 and not accuracy, and why
@sec-classification-metrics returns to the point with more force.

**The whole sweep costs under four seconds.** Every fit in that column takes
about a second or less on a laptop CPU, three seconds in total. Whatever else is true about the sparse baseline,
you can afford to run it, and you should run it before you believe any number
from anything more expensive.

::: {.column-margin}
The `features` column is a reminder of what tf-idf actually is. At 200 labels
there are 720 surviving n-grams, because `min_df=2` discards everything seen
once. The model is not "small" by choice; it is small because the vocabulary it
is allowed to see is small. That is also why it degrades so gracefully — there
is nothing to overfit.
:::

## Fine-tuning encoder models {#sec-classification-finetune}

The competitor is BERTurk, the Turkish BERT released as
`dbmdz/bert-base-turkish-cased` [@schweter2020berturk].

::: {.column-margin}
BERTurk is a 2020 checkpoint. We use it because it is the strongest
widely-used *Turkish-specific* encoder — not because it is the frontier. The 2024–2026 encoder revival rebuilt the same
110M-parameter budget with rotary embeddings, unpadding and an 8,192-token
context: ModernBERT [@warner2025modernbert] and the multilingual families that
followed it cover Turkish and train markedly faster. Either of this chapter's
cost headlines would move on one of them. We did not re-run the sweep, which is
the honest boundary of the 970× figure.
:::

BERTurk was pretrained on roughly 35 GB and 4.4 billion tokens of Turkish — filtered OSCAR, a Wikipedia
dump, OPUS corpora, and a corpus contributed by Kemal Oflazer — with a
32,000-token vocabulary, on a TPU v3-8.

::: {.column-margin}
The model card says 2M training steps; the repository's cheat-sheet passes
`--num_train_steps=3000000`. We could not resolve which is right, so the chapter
does not depend on it. The model card also prints the token count as
"44,04,976,662", a digit-grouping typo for 4,404,976,662 — a small reminder that
model cards are prose, not data.
:::

Loading the checkpoint and counting gives **110,618,882 parameters**: 24,972,288
in the embedding table, 85,054,464 in the twelve encoder layers, 590,592 in the
pooler, and the remaining 1,538 in the two-class classification head
($768 \times 2$ weights plus two biases) that replaces the pretraining head we
throw away. Those four add up exactly. That embedding
number is worth pausing on — 22.6% of the model is a lookup table, and it exists
because the vocabulary is 32,000 tokens wide.

### The sequence-length decision, made with a measurement

Attention is quadratic in sequence length (@sec-transformers), so `max_length` is
the single biggest lever on training cost. The usual advice is 512, which is the
model's limit. Here is what the corpus actually needs, in BERTurk subwords:

```text
median    29 subwords
p95       86
p99      146
max      466

truncated at max_length=64    10.97% of documents
truncated at max_length=128    1.54%
truncated at max_length=192    0.36%
truncated at max_length=256    0.11%
truncated at max_length=512    0.00%
```

Those counts are over the 40,000-document training slice and include the
`[CLS]` and `[SEP]` tokens, because that is what the GPU actually pads and
truncates. The test slice behaves the same way — median 29, p95 87 — so the
decision does not depend on which slice you measure.

We use 128. It truncates 1.54% of reviews and costs a *sixteenth* of the
attention compute of 512. [Picking 512 "to be safe" would have quadrupled the
sequence length to protect fewer than two documents in a hundred, and those
documents are long precisely because they ramble.]{.hl} The five-minute measurement that
produced this table is the highest-return five minutes in the chapter.

### The learning curve

Same budgets, same subsets, same test set. Class-weighted cross-entropy, AdamW at
2e-5, batch 32, `max_length` 128, linear warmup over the first 10% of steps.
Budgets of 2,000 and below get 20 epochs, larger budgets get 3 — otherwise the
small runs would see so few gradient updates that we would be measuring the
budget schedule rather than the budget.

```text
labels   macro-F1   complaint-F1   complaint-P   complaint-R   steps
   200      54.31          12.83         20.49          9.33     140
   500      56.46          16.37         40.12         10.29     320
 1,000      71.57          45.95         63.76         35.92     640
 2,000      79.61          61.63         66.48         57.44   1,260
 5,000      81.27          65.12         60.22         70.89     471
10,000      82.71          67.50         71.30         64.08     939
20,000      83.71          69.41         72.26         66.77   1,875
40,000      85.02          71.92         72.32         71.52   3,750
```

**Two caveats before you read the numbers, and the first is about what is not
here.** Every point on this curve is a single training run at a single seed. At
the small budgets that matters most: with a randomly initialised classification
head and 500 examples, macro-F1 varies by seed on a scale of points, so the
15.1-point jump between 500 and 1,000 labels is a jump we have measured once.
Three seeds at 500, 1,000 and 2,000 would put an error bar on the crossover and
it is the measurement this section most needs. Note also what the bootstrap
intervals later in this chapter measure. A bootstrap interval redraws the test
documents with replacement many times, recomputes the metric on each redraw,
and reports the middle 95% of the values. It resamples the *test set*, not the
optimiser, so it describes evaluation noise and says nothing about training
noise.

**The second caveat is one the `steps` column makes visible.** The epoch
schedule changes at 2,000, so the 2,000-label model gets 1,260 updates and the
5,000-label model only 471 — nearly **seven times** more gradient updates per
example. That is the most likely reason complaint precision *falls* from 66.48
to 60.22 across that one step, and why the 5,000-label model scores *below* the
2,000-label one on the shared subsample in @sec-classification-llm (81.21
against 82.00). A learning curve that dips as the budget grows is not normal,
and a schedule change is the first thing to suspect. Both of this chapter's
headline crossovers sit at exactly the budget that got the most training per
example. We did not re-run 5,000 at 20 epochs to separate the two, so read every
crossover below as *at this schedule*.

Three readings, and the third is the one that changes how you plan a project.

**The encoder loses at the bottom of the curve.** At 200 labels BERTurk scores
54.31 against tf-idf's 55.46; at 500 it scores 56.46 against 60.82. A
110-million-parameter model pretrained on 4.4 billion tokens of Turkish is
*worse* than a bag of words, on Turkish, with 500 examples. Nothing is wrong: the
classification head is randomly initialised and 500 examples containing 32
complaints is not enough signal to move a network that size into a useful region
without overfitting first.

**The crossover is between 500 and 1,000 labels**, and it is abrupt. Across that
one doubling BERTurk gains 15.1 macro-F1 points and tf-idf gains 0.8. Complaint
recall goes from 10.29% to 35.92%. Somewhere in there the model stops predicting
the majority class with occasional accidents and starts having a representation
of what a complaint is.

**BERTurk at 2,000 labels beats tf-idf at 40,000.** [79.61 against 76.21 — twenty
times fewer labels for a better model.]{.hl} If labelling is your bottleneck, and
it usually is, that ratio is the number to take to a planning meeting. At equal
budget the gap is 8.81 macro-F1 points and **15.45 points of complaint-F1**,
which is the number a person actually experiences.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bertRows = [
  {n: 200,   bert: 54.31, bert_negf1: 12.83, tfidf: 55.46, tfidf_negf1: 14.63, steps: 140},
  {n: 500,   bert: 56.46, bert_negf1: 16.37, tfidf: 60.82, tfidf_negf1: 25.32, steps: 320},
  {n: 1000,  bert: 71.57, bert_negf1: 45.95, tfidf: 61.60, tfidf_negf1: 27.03, steps: 640},
  {n: 2000,  bert: 79.61, bert_negf1: 61.63, tfidf: 67.42, tfidf_negf1: 38.77, steps: 1260},
  {n: 5000,  bert: 81.27, bert_negf1: 65.12, tfidf: 72.77, tfidf_negf1: 49.18, steps: 471},
```

::: {.column-margin}
The teal rule marks the crossover region. Switch to **complaint F1** and notice
that the two curves cross in the same place but the gap afterwards is roughly
twice as wide: at 40,000 labels macro-F1 differs by 8.81 points and complaint-F1
by 15.45. Averaging over a 93.7%-majority class hides most of what the encoder
bought you.
:::

### What the sweep cost, and which of those numbers we trust

Training cost is measured in optimiser steps, which is reproducible, and in
seconds, which is not — and this run is a good illustration of why the
distinction matters.

```text
labels   steps   wall-clock   s/step
 1,000     640       525.5s    0.821   ← first GPU run after a cold start
 2,000   1,260       387.0s    0.307
 5,000     471       147.5s    0.313
10,000     939       289.5s    0.308
20,000   1,875       581.5s    0.310
40,000   3,750     6,303.1s    1.681   ← machine slowed mid-run
```

Four consecutive runs agree on **0.307 to 0.313 seconds per step** at batch 32
and `max_length` 128. That is a real measurement: four independent runs spanning
a tenfold range of dataset size (2,000 to 20,000 labels), agreeing within 2%. The other two are not.
The 1,000-label run paid a one-off Metal kernel-compilation cost, and the
40,000-label run took 386 seconds for its first epoch, 386 for its second, and
**5,531 for its third** — a 14× slowdown with no change in the work being done.

So the honest statement is: [at 0.31 s/step the whole eight-point sweep is 9,395
steps, about 49 minutes of GPU time, and the 40,000-label model on its own is
about 19 minutes.]{.hl} The 6,303 seconds we actually observed is a fact about
the laptop that evening, not about the model, and quoting it as a training cost
would mislead every reader who tried to reproduce it.

::: {.column-margin}
Inference is much better behaved: 499, 434, 462, 472, 466, 475 and 510 documents
per second across seven runs, on the same 10,000 documents each time. Call it **470
documents per second**, single process, batched, on a laptop GPU. Only the
200-label run disagrees, at 17.5 — that was the first inference pass of the whole
session, and it was paying for kernel compilation on behalf of everything after
it. [When one measurement in a series is 27× off, suspect your harness before
your model.]{.hl}
:::

Compare against the sparse baseline, whose whole eight-point sweep fits in three
seconds of laptop CPU. At the top budget that is 3,750 steps × 0.31 s — 1,162
seconds of corrected GPU time, *not* the 6,303 the contaminated run recorded —
against 1.2 seconds for the vectoriser. The encoder is roughly
**970× more expensive to train** for 8.81 macro-F1 points, and serves about 470
documents per second against tens of thousands. Whether that is a good trade is
not a machine-learning question; @sec-classification-crossover is where we try
to answer it with money.

## Metrics beyond accuracy {#sec-classification-metrics}

Every number so far has been macro-F1, on the assertion — inherited from
@sec-bake-off — that accuracy is useless on this corpus. It is time to show that
rather than assert it.

Take one model, the uncorrected tf-idf baseline, and move nothing except the
threshold at which it declares a review a complaint. "Uncorrected" means no
class weights, and this copy is fitted on the 32,000-document `fit` slice so
that `cal` stays clean — so it is not the class-weighted 76.21 model above.
@sec-classification-imbalance uses the same fitted model. The table below is read on
**`test`**, and it is illustration rather than selection: it exists to show what
the metrics do across the range, not to pick an operating point. The operating
point actually used in @sec-classification-imbalance was chosen on `cal` and
lands at 0.166 — one grid step from the best row here, which is roughly the
regret you should expect from doing it properly.

```text
   t      acc   bal-acc    prec     rec   compF1   macroF1     MCC
0.05    68.98     81.53   16.46   95.89    28.09     54.16   0.318
0.10    89.21     85.76   34.91   81.80    48.94     71.45   0.490
0.15    94.23     81.06   53.53   65.98    59.11     78.00   0.564
0.20    95.00     73.28   63.75   48.42    55.04     76.19   0.530
0.25    95.16     68.57   72.16   38.13    49.90     73.68   0.503
0.30    95.00     64.57   77.05   29.75    42.92     70.15   0.460
0.40    94.59     58.90   83.21   18.04    29.65     63.42   0.372
0.50    94.28     55.41   88.46   10.92    19.44     58.24   0.299
0.60    94.07     53.31   93.33    6.65    12.41     54.67   0.240
0.70    93.94     52.13   96.43    4.27     8.18     52.52   0.196
0.80    93.77     50.71  100.00    1.42     2.81     49.79   0.116
0.95    93.70     50.16  100.00    0.32     0.63     48.69   0.054
```

Read the accuracy column top to bottom over the range $t \ge 0.2$. It moves from
95.00 to 93.70 — **1.3 points**, and never spans more than 1.5. Over the same range, recall on the class
somebody has to act on falls from 48.42% to 0.32%, and complaint-F1 falls from
55.04 to 0.63. [A metric that changes by one point while the system goes from
catching half the complaints to catching none of them is not measuring the
system.]{.hl}

Worse than useless, it is actively misleading. The *highest* accuracy in the
table is 95.16 at $t = 0.25$. The best model in the table is at $t = 0.15$ — an
*oracle*, by the rule in @sec-classification-setup, since we are reading the
maximum off the test set —
where macro-F1 is 78.00 and accuracy is 0.93 points *lower*. Tuning on accuracy
picks the wrong operating point, and it does so confidently.

The widget below plots the whole table. Accuracy is drawn in grey behind every
selection, so whatever you switch to, you are looking at it against the metric
that does not move.

::: {.column-margin}
The faint red rule at 48.37 is the macro-F1 of a model that always answers
"satisfied". Switch the radio to **macro-F1** and watch the blue line dive
towards it as the threshold rises: past $t = 0.8$ the model has effectively
stopped being a classifier, and accuracy is still 93.77.
:::

The reason is arithmetic, not philosophy:

```text
call everything satisfied      acc 93.68   macroF1 48.37   bal-acc 50.00   MCC  0.000
guess at the base rate         acc 87.98   macroF1 49.76   bal-acc 49.76   MCC -0.005
call everything a complaint    acc  6.32   macroF1  5.94   bal-acc 50.00   MCC  0.000
coin flip                      acc 50.21   macroF1 38.57   bal-acc 51.44   MCC  0.014
```

A model that has never seen a feature scores 93.68% accuracy — the
[base rate](#gloss-base-rate){#term-base-rate .term-ref}. Every accuracy figure
in this chapter has to be read against that floor, and most of them are within
two points of it. **Matthews correlation** (MCC), by contrast, gives every
no-skill row in that table zero or within 0.02 of it — exactly 0.000 for the two
constant predictors — which is what you want from a summary statistic. The
chapter leans on it more than once, so here is what it is: the Pearson
correlation between the predicted and the true label, treated as two 0/1
variables,

$$
\mathrm{MCC} = \frac{TP \cdot TN - FP \cdot FN}
{\sqrt{(TP{+}FP)(TP{+}FN)(TN{+}FP)(TN{+}FN)}}
$$

running from $-1$ to $+1$. Be precise about the zero, because it is the whole
reason to reach for this metric. For a **constant** predictor the denominator
is zero — a model that always answers *positive* has $TN = FN = 0$ — so MCC is
$0/0$, undefined, and `scikit-learn` returns 0 by convention. For a predictor
that guesses at random, independently of the input, the *expected* MCC is 0 and
the observed value fluctuates around it with the sample size. Either way the
answer is "about nothing", which is precisely what accuracy fails to say here.

**One metric is missing from that table on purpose, and it is the one you will
meet first.** `classification_report` prints **weighted-F1** by default: the
per-class F1 scores averaged by *support*. On this corpus the support is 93.68%
one class, so the always-satisfied model's weighted-F1 is
$0.9368 \times 96.74 = 90.62$ — higher than any macro-F1 anywhere in this
chapter, for a model with no features. Weighted-F1 is accuracy wearing an F1
costume. **Micro-F1** — pool the $TP$, $FP$ and $FN$ counts of all classes, then
compute one F1 — is worse still: when every document gets exactly one label it
*equals* accuracy, 93.68 here. If you report one number on imbalanced data, report macro-F1 or MCC;
if you report weighted-F1, print the majority-class rate next to it so the
reader can do the subtraction.

::: {#gloss-base-rate .column-margin .term-gloss}
**base rate** — how much of the corpus belongs to a class. It doubles as the
accuracy of a model that always answers with the majority, which makes it the
first number to compute and the last one anybody reports.
[↩](#term-base-rate){.term-back}
:::

### ROC and precision-recall are not interchangeable

Both curves are computed from exactly the same
[confusion matrices](#gloss-confusion-matrix){#term-confusion-matrix .term-ref}.
They disagree
because they divide by different things: the false-positive rate divides by the
9,368 satisfied reviews, while precision divides by however many documents you
flagged [@davis2006relationship].

::: {#gloss-confusion-matrix .column-margin .term-gloss}
**confusion matrix** — the four counts a binary classifier produces: true
positives, false positives, false negatives, true negatives. Every metric in
this chapter is some arithmetic on those four numbers, which is why two metrics
can disagree without either being wrong.
[↩](#term-confusion-matrix){.term-back}
:::

```text
model                          AP      AUC   AP/base   bal-acc     MCC
tf-idf, uncorrected         60.30    93.24     9.54x     55.41   0.299
tf-idf, class-weighted      60.81    93.44     9.62x     84.34   0.545
tf-idf, SMOTE               58.05    92.81     9.19x     82.03   0.514
BERTurk n=200               12.78    70.12     2.02x     53.45   0.100
BERTurk n=500               26.98    83.00     4.27x     54.62   0.178
BERTurk n=1,000             45.72    82.76     7.23x     67.27   0.454
BERTurk n=2,000             62.34    92.51     9.86x     77.74   0.594
BERTurk n=5,000             66.37    93.98    10.50x     83.86   0.628
```

AUC, the area under the ROC curve, has a plain reading worth keeping: it is the
probability that a randomly chosen complaint gets a higher score than a randomly
chosen satisfied review, with ties counted as half. It looks only at the
*order* of the scores, never at a threshold.

An AUC of 93.24 sounds like a solved problem. The
[average precision](#gloss-average-precision){#term-average-precision .term-ref}
for the same model and the same scores is 60.30. Both are correct. The AUC is
high because the model is very good at the easy majority of the ranking, and the
false positive rate has 9,368 documents in its denominator to hide mistakes in.

::: {#gloss-average-precision .column-margin .term-gloss}
**average precision** — the area under the precision-recall curve, written *AP*.
Unlike AUC it moves with the class balance, so an AP of 60.30 means nothing
until you know that guessing at random would score 6.32.
[↩](#term-average-precision){.term-back}
:::

The clearest evidence that these are different measurements is BERTurk between
500 and 1,000 labels: [AUC goes **down** (83.00 → 82.76) while average precision
goes **up** by 18.7 points (26.98 → 45.72)]{.hl} and macro-F1 goes up by 15.1.
If you had been watching AUC you would have concluded the extra 500 labels made
the model worse.

The widget below draws exactly those two disagreeing views. Switch between ROC
space and PR space with the same models selected and watch the ordering of the
curves change.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
```
```{ojs}
rocNames = ({
  tfidf: "tf-idf + LR, uncorrected, 32,000 labels", b500: "BERTurk, 500 labels",
  b1000: "BERTurk, 1,000 labels", b5000: "BERTurk, 5,000 labels"
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
rocPlot = {
  const data = curveRows.filter(d => d.space === rocSpace);
  const isRoc = rocSpace === "roc";
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 640,
    height: 440,
    marginLeft: 60,
    marginBottom: 48,
    x: { label: isRoc ? "false-positive rate — of 9,368 satisfied reviews, the share flagged"
                      : "recall — of 632 complaints, the share caught",
         domain: [0, 1], grid: true },
    y: { label: isRoc ? "true-positive rate — of 632 complaints, the share caught"
                      : "precision — of what was flagged, the share that was right",
         domain: [0, 1], grid: true },
    color: { legend: true, domain: ["tfidf", "b500", "b1000", "b5000"],
             range: ["#1F4E79", "#C08A3E", "#B3453E", "#0E7C7B"],
             tickFormat: k => rocNames[k] },
    marks: [
      isRoc
        ? Plot.line([[0, 0], [1, 1]], { stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "5 4" })
        : Plot.ruleY([0.0632], { stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "5 4" }),
      Plot.line(data, { x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "model", strokeWidth: 2 })
    ]
  });
}
```

::: {.column-margin}
The dashed line means something different in each space. In ROC space it is the
diagonal a coin flip traces. In PR space it is the horizontal line at **0.0632**
— the base rate, which is what precision equals when you flag documents at
random. Notice how much of the ROC plot sits far above its baseline and how
little of the PR plot does. Same models, same scores.
:::

The `AP/base` column is the honest way to read average precision: 60.30 against
a 6.32% base rate is 9.54× better than random, which is a real achievement that
"60" does not convey on its own.

## Class imbalance {#sec-classification-imbalance}

The corpus is 93.68% satisfied. The standard menu of responses to that
[class imbalance](#gloss-class-imbalance){#term-class-imbalance .term-ref} is:
do nothing, weight the classes, oversample the minority, undersample the
majority, or synthesise new minority points with SMOTE [@chawla2002smote],
which creates each synthetic point on the straight line between a minority
example and one of its nearest minority neighbours. There is a sixth option that is usually listed last and treated as a hack, and
it wins.

::: {#gloss-class-imbalance .column-margin .term-gloss}
**class imbalance** — one label dominates the corpus, so accuracy stops carrying
information and the loss function stops caring about the class you built the
system for. It is a property of the data, not a bug in it.
[↩](#term-class-imbalance){.term-back}
:::

Everything below is fitted on the 32,000-document `fit` slice, with any
threshold chosen on the held-out `cal` slice, and scored on `test`.

```text
treatment                     acc   macroF1   compF1   comp-P   comp-R      AP     AUC
no correction, t=0.5        94.28     58.24    19.44     88.5     10.9   60.30   93.24
threshold moved to 0.166    94.64     77.66    58.19     57.4     59.0   60.30   93.24
class_weight=balanced       92.63     76.09    56.21     45.0     74.8   60.81   93.44
random oversampling         93.63     77.63    58.72     49.7     71.7   61.46   93.45
random undersampling        81.08     62.98    37.10     23.5     88.3   52.49   92.15
SMOTE                       92.32     74.72    53.62     43.4     70.3   58.05   92.81
```

::: {.fig-cap}
The axis starts at 45, not 0, because a model with no features scores 48.37 and
everything interesting happens above it. The `AP` column is the control: average
precision depends only on the ranking, so the same fitted model read at two
thresholds must show the same AP — which rows 1 and 2 do, to four significant
figures.
:::
::::

Row two is the whole section. **The same model as row one** — not retrained, not
reweighted, not resampled, the identical fitted coefficients — goes from 58.24
to 77.66 macro-F1 because we flagged a review when $P(\text{complaint})$ passed
0.166 instead of 0.5.

The proof that nothing about the model changed is in the last two columns.
Average precision and AUC are *identical* to four significant figures in rows
one and two, because both are computed from the ranking, and moving a threshold
cannot reorder anything. [The four retraining treatments — class weights,
oversampling, undersampling, SMOTE — are attempts to change a ranking in order
to fix a decision. Moving the threshold fixes the decision directly.]{.hl}

**One thing the table does not do fairly, and you should hold it against the
headline.** Only one of the six rows was allowed to choose its threshold; the
other five are read at 0.5. That is a tuned arm racing untuned ones. The
chapter's own argument says how it would come out otherwise: average precision
depends only on the ranking, and the ranking is oversampling 61.46, class
weights 60.81, uncorrected 60.30 — so if every arm were given its own threshold
on `cal`, oversampling would probably end up marginally *ahead*, not behind. We
did not run those three rows. **Read this section as a result about price, not
about ranking:** moving one threshold buys the same operating point the best
resampling method buys, at zero training cost — it does not beat it.

Against that, the retraining methods look expensive at the price they charge:

- **Class weights** reach 76.09, 1.57 points *below* the free option, and cost a
  refit.
- **Random oversampling** reaches 77.63, within three hundredths of a point of
  moving the threshold, on 59,954 rows instead of 32,000 — nearly double the
  training time for what looks like a tie. We did not test that gap formally,
  and a 0.03-point difference is far below what a test set with 632 complaints
  can resolve, so "indistinguishable" is all the table entitles us to say.
- **Random undersampling** is a disaster: 62.98. It threw away 27,954 of 32,000
  documents to achieve parity, and the majority class it discarded was carrying
  most of the information about what a *non*-complaint looks like. Precision
  collapses to 23.5%.
- **SMOTE** reaches 74.72, worse than doing nothing but moving the threshold,
  and worse than class weights.

::: {.column-margin}
SMOTE's poor showing here is not a refutation of the paper, and the chapter
should not pretend it is. Chawla et al. evaluated nine low-dimensional dense
numeric datasets — Pima, Phoneme, Adult, Satimage and so on — and explicitly
listed text as *future work*, noting it "would have to be applied in conjunction
with a feature selection algorithm" [@chawla2002smote]. Interpolating between
two sparse tf-idf rows — 83,281 dimensions here rather than the 101,659 quoted
elsewhere, because this section fits on the 32,000-document `fit` slice rather
than the full 40,000 — produces a point that corresponds to no document anyone
could write. We measured it because it is what practitioners
reach for, not because the authors claimed it would work here.
:::

This is not a quirk of this corpus. Van den Goorbergh and colleagues found the
same thing on clinical risk models, and put it more sharply than we would dare:
imbalance corrections buy nothing in discrimination and do real damage
elsewhere [@vandengoorbergh2022harm]. @sec-classification-calibration measures
the damage.

Elkan's paper — the one everyone cites in the neighbourhood of this
topic — argues the same way, and it is worth quoting the recommendation
correctly because it is routinely inverted. Elkan's advice is to *learn a
classifier from the training set as given, and then compute optimal decisions
explicitly* [@elkan2001foundations]. His paper is an argument **against**
resampling, not for it.

## Is that number a probability? {#sec-classification-calibration}

Moving the threshold works. But it raises a question the previous section
quietly skipped: 0.166 came from a sweep on held-out data. If you wanted to
*derive* a threshold instead — from a cost matrix, say — you would need the
model's output to mean something. So: when the classifier says a review is 0.834
likely to be satisfied, is that a probability?

Everything here is fitted on the 8,000-document `cal` slice, which no model in
this section was trained on, and scored on `test`. That separation is the whole
point — and it is why the BERTurk row below is a model trained on the 32,000-
document `fit` slice rather than the 40,000-document `train` that produced the
learning curve. A calibrator fitted on documents the classifier already fits
well reports that the classifier is calibrated when it is not.

Four statistics in the table need a sentence each. All of them compare the
predicted probability of *satisfied* with what actually happened. **ECE**
(expected calibration error) sorts the test documents into fifteen equal-width
bins by predicted probability, takes the gap between each bin's mean prediction
and the fraction of that bin that really was satisfied, and averages the gaps
weighted by bin size; it is printed in percentage points. **MCE** (maximum
calibration error) is the largest of those gaps, whatever the bin size. The
**Brier score** is the mean squared difference between the predicted
probability and the 0/1 outcome, and **log loss** is the mean of $-\log$ of the
probability the model gave to the label that actually occurred. For all four,
lower is better, and the last two need no bins at all. The three repairs are
all fitted on `cal`. Writing $z$ for the model's logit and $\sigma$ for the
logistic sigmoid: **temperature scaling** fits one number $T$ and outputs
$\sigma(z/T)$; **Platt scaling** fits a slope and an intercept and outputs
$\sigma(az + b)$; **isotonic regression** fits any map that never goes down.

```text
model / method                       ECE    MCE    Brier   logloss   mean p
tf-idf, no correction — raw         3.96  39.32   0.0421    0.1514    0.940
  — temperature                     3.20  39.36   0.0426    0.1489    0.952
  — Platt                           0.94  16.58   0.0368    0.1318    0.935
  — isotonic                        0.69  32.96   0.0367    0.1309    0.935
  — isotonic fitted on TRAIN        2.39  24.66   0.0387    0.1487    0.942

tf-idf, class-weighted — raw       14.18  35.93   0.0675    0.2448    0.795
  — temperature                     7.80  43.29   0.0568    0.1974    0.859
  — Platt                           0.93  15.28   0.0364    0.1300    0.935
  — isotonic                        0.88  72.20   0.0364    0.1295    0.935

BERTurk, class-weighted — raw       2.53  49.84   0.0318    0.1442    0.933
  — temperature                     2.58  50.02   0.0303    0.1224    0.913
  — Platt                           1.25  31.65   0.0275    0.1062    0.936
  — isotonic                        0.56  45.84   0.0265    0.0984    0.936
```

**Every ECE in that table carries an estimator floor, and several of the
differences are below it.** ECE compares an observed frequency against a mean
prediction inside each bin, and an observed frequency is a binomial draw: even
with perfect calibration the two differ by chance. With our bin occupancies that
noise alone produces an expected $|\text{ECE}|$ of about **half a point**. So
Platt's 0.94 against isotonic's 0.69 — a gap of 0.25 — is not a measurement of a
difference between the two methods, and neither is BERTurk's 0.56, which is not
distinguishable from perfect. What *does* survive the floor is the raw-versus-
calibrated gap (3.96 → 0.9) and the class-weighting penalty (3.96 → 14.18), both
an order of magnitude above it. Estimating ECE without bias is its own small
literature [@kumar2019verified; @roelofs2022mitigating]; the practical rule is
to distrust any calibration difference smaller than about a point unless you
have bootstrapped it.

Those numbers are summaries of a picture, and the picture is more informative
than the summary. Each dot below is one of the fifteen bins, plotted at its mean
predicted probability against the fraction of that bin that really was
satisfied. Perfect calibration is the diagonal. Dot area is the number of
documents in the bin, because a bin holding three documents and a bin holding
7,317 should not look equally important.

```{ojs}
  // only the uncorrected linear model has the deliberately-leaked calibrator
  const avail = relModel === "plain"
    ? ["raw", "temp", "platt", "iso", "leak"]
    : ["raw", "temp", "platt", "iso"];
  const keep = relPick.filter(m => avail.includes(m));

    r: { range: [2, 14] },
    color: { legend: true, domain: ["raw", "temp", "platt", "iso", "leak"],

      Plot.dot(data, { x: "conf", y: "freq", fill: "method", r: "n", fillOpacity: 0.75,
        title: d => `${names[d.method]}\npredicted ${(100*d.conf).toFixed(1)}%\n` +

```

::: {.column-margin}
Switch the model to **class_weight=balanced** and leave only **raw** ticked. The
whole curve sits above the diagonal: every bin contains more satisfied reviews
than the model predicted. That is not noise, it is a systematic downward shift
of every probability, and it is what the next few paragraphs are about.
:::

The true base rate on test is 0.9368. Five findings, in order of how surprising
they are.

**Class weighting destroys calibration.** ECE goes from 3.96 to 14.18, a 3.6×
increase, and the model's mean predicted probability drops to 0.795 against a
true rate of 0.9368. The reweighted model is *better* by macro-F1 (76.09 vs
58.24) and its probabilities are far worse. [If your model's output is going to
be shown to a human, or multiplied by a cost, or thresholded by a rule somebody
else writes, class weighting silently breaks all three.]{.hl} This is
van den Goorbergh et al.'s result, reproduced on text.

**Temperature scaling gets halfway at best**, and that is structural rather than
bad luck. Temperature has one parameter and it preserves the ranking and the
argmax; in a binary problem it can only push probabilities toward 0.5 or toward
the extremes, symmetrically about the 0.5 cut. What is wrong with the
class-weighted model is a *shifted prior* — it thinks complaints are commoner
than they are — and that needs every logit moved by the same amount, not
stretched. Temperature can move the mean only as a side effect of sharpening:
here it lifts the mean prediction from 0.795 to 0.859 and ECE falls from 14.18
to 7.80, and then it has no parameter left. Platt scaling has two parameters, a slope and an intercept
[@platt1999probabilistic], and the intercept is exactly the knob that fixes a
prior shift. It takes ECE from 14.18 to 0.93.

::: {.column-margin}
Guo et al. popularised temperature scaling and found it to be a strong baseline
on image classifiers [@guo2017calibration]. That is not in tension with this
result: their networks were overconfident but not systematically shifted, which
is the failure temperature is designed for. Reaching for temperature scaling
here is reaching for a one-parameter fix to a two-parameter problem.
:::

**ECE and MCE disagree, and neither is enough on its own.**
[Isotonic regression](#gloss-isotonic-regression){#term-isotonic-regression .term-ref}
on the class-weighted model gets the best ECE of its group (0.88) and the
*worst* MCE in the table (72.20). ECE is an $n$-weighted average, so a single
sparse bin with a large gap barely moves it. MCE ignores bin size, so a single
sparse bin decides it — and here that bin holds **one document**, which the
isotonic map put at 0.278 and which happened to be satisfied. The next-worst
gap for the same model is 9.0 points, in a bin of 40. So 72.20 describes one
review, not the tail: the binomial noise that puts a floor under ECE puts a far
higher one under MCE. If your decisions live in the tail — and cost-sensitive
decisions usually do — the average is the wrong summary, and the maximum is a
noisy one. Look at the reliability diagram *with its bin counts*, which is what
the dot sizes in the widget above are for.

::: {#gloss-isotonic-regression .column-margin .term-gloss}
**isotonic regression** — fits the calibration map as a free staircase that is
only required to never go down. It can bend into any monotone shape a sigmoid
cannot, which is why it wins with enough held-out data and overfits without it.
[↩](#term-isotonic-regression){.term-back}
:::

**Fitting the calibrator on training data does not look broken.** The row marked
"isotonic fitted on TRAIN" is the mistake this section exists to warn about: we
fitted the isotonic map on the same 32,000 documents the classifier was trained
on. It scores ECE 2.39. That is 3.5× worse than fitting it properly on held-out
data (0.69) — and still *better than doing nothing* (3.96). [The leak does not
produce an obviously wrong number. It produces a plausible number that is
silently several times worse than the one you could have had]{.hl}, which is why
it survives code review.

**The transformer is better calibrated on average and worse in the tail.**
BERTurk's raw ECE is 2.53 against the linear model's 3.96, its Brier score is
0.0318 against 0.0421, and its mean prediction of 0.933 is within four
thousandths of the true base rate. So the folk claim that deep networks are
wildly overconfident does not reproduce here in the aggregate. What does
reproduce is in the other column: [BERTurk's *maximum* calibration error is
49.84, the worst raw figure in the table]{.hl}. Somewhere there is a bin where
the model says one thing and the data says something 50 points away — and
@sec-classification-errors will show you exactly which documents live there.
Calibrating fixes the average (isotonic takes ECE to 0.56 — indistinguishable
from perfect at this bin structure, and with the best Brier and log loss in the
chapter, which are the statistics that *are* sharp here). Its MCE stays at
45.84, but after calibration that figure comes from a bin holding a single
document, so it says little. The raw model's tail is the real finding: its
three worst bins, holding 11, 13 and 20 documents, are between 44.7 and 49.8
points off.

::: {.column-margin}
This BERTurk was fine-tuned on the 32,000-document `fit` slice, not the 40,000
of `train`, precisely so that `cal` stays untouched. That makes it a slightly
weaker classifier than the one in @sec-classification-finetune — 84.45 macro-F1
against 85.02, which is what 8,000 fewer labels buys — and the only honest one
to calibrate. Reusing the 40,000-label model here would have fitted
the calibrator on 8,000 documents it had already been trained on — the exact
leak the "isotonic on TRAIN" row measures.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
This is Platt's own warning, and it is usually overstated. He does not say never
fit on the training set; he says that for *nonlinear* SVMs it "sometimes leads to
disastrously biased fits", and that for linear models "it is often possible to
simply fit the sigmoid on the training set". Our model is linear, and indeed the
leak here is bad but not disastrous. The remedy he recommends is three-fold
cross-validation, with a hold-out of "typically 30%" as the cheaper alternative
[@platt1999probabilistic].
:::

### A note on which ECE

Expected calibration error is not one statistic. Guo et al. bin on the
**top-label** confidence $\max_k p_k$ and ask how often the `argmax` is right
[@guo2017calibration]. In a binary problem that quantity lives in $[0.5, 1]$, so
half the bins are empty by construction, and the number is not comparable to
binning on $P(\text{class } 1)$ directly. Both are reported by our measurement
code; the table above uses the binary version, and the top-label version is
systematically smaller — 8.98 rather than 14.18 for the class-weighted model.

The choice is not cosmetic, and applying temperature scaling to BERTurk shows
why. On the binary statistic it makes things marginally worse, 2.53 → **2.58**.
On the top-label statistic it looks like a large win, 2.47 → **0.73**. Same
model, same fitted temperature, same test set, one operation — reported as a
3.4× improvement or a small regression depending purely on which ECE you print.
Both numbers are correct, and they are answering different questions: how well
the probability of *satisfied* is calibrated, versus how well the confidence in
whichever label won is calibrated. [Quoting an ECE without saying which one you
computed is wrong.]{.hl}

There is a second degree of freedom, and on this corpus it is the larger one:
**how many bins, and how they are drawn.** Ours are fifteen of equal width, and
on a distribution this skewed the top bin holds 73% of the test set while ten
bins hold fewer than a hundred documents each — so the statistic is decided by a
handful of bins. Equal-mass (adaptive) binning puts the same number of documents
in every bin and gives a different number for the same model
[@nixon2019measuring]. Both schemes are biased upward by binomial noise, which
is where the half-point floor above comes from, and there are estimators
designed to reduce it [@kumar2019verified; @roelofs2022mitigating]. Report the
bin count, the binning scheme, and — if the difference you are claiming is under
a point — a bootstrap interval.

## Choosing the threshold from a cost matrix {#sec-classification-costs}

Now the payoff. If the model's output is a probability, you do not have to sweep
for a threshold — you can derive one.

Let $q = P(\text{complaint} \mid x)$, and suppose a false alarm costs
$C_{FP}$ and a missed complaint costs $C_{FN}$. Flagging costs
$(1-q) \cdot C_{FP}$; letting it pass costs $q \cdot C_{FN}$. Flagging is worth
it when

$$q > \frac{C_{FP}}{C_{FN} + C_{FP}} = \frac{1}{1+r}, \qquad r = \frac{C_{FN}}{C_{FP}}$$

That is Elkan's threshold [@elkan2001foundations], and it comes with a condition
that gets dropped every time it is quoted: [$q$ has to be a probability]{.hl}.
Here is what happens when it is not. Costs are in units of $C_{FP} = 1$, on the
10,000-document test set; "oracle" is the best possible threshold found by
sweeping on test itself, so every row has a regret.

```text
  r    Elkan q*    raw    calibrated   swept    oracle | regret: raw   calib   swept
  1      0.5000    572           501     498       483 |      18.4%    3.7%    3.1%
  2      0.3333    980           797     792       776 |      26.3%    2.7%    2.1%
  5      0.1667   1575          1357    1357      1342 |      17.4%    1.1%    1.1%
 10      0.0909   2218          2173    2167      2052 |       8.1%    5.9%    5.6%
 25      0.0385   4395          3551    3558      3479 |      26.3%    2.1%    2.3%
 50      0.0196   6764          4626    4546      4345 |      55.7%    6.5%    4.6%
100      0.0099   8373          5645    5647      5416 |      54.6%    4.2%    4.3%
```

Applying the correct formula to uncalibrated scores overspends by 8% to 56%.
Applying it to isotonic-calibrated scores from the same model overspends by 1%
to 7%. The formula was never the problem.

The mechanism is visible in the flagging counts. At $r = 100$ the raw model
raises 8,073 false alarms against 9,368 satisfied reviews — it flags 86% of the
happy customers — because its scores are compressed into a region where a
threshold of 0.0099 catches nearly everything. The calibrated model raises 3,345
false alarms and misses 23 complaints instead of 3. Both catch almost every
complaint; one drowns the team in false alarms to do it.

```{ojs}
    ["r = 1 — a false alarm and a missed complaint cost the same", 1],
    ["r = 2", 2],
    ["r = 5 — a missed complaint costs five false alarms", 5],
    ["r = 10", 10],
    ["r = 25", 25],
    ["r = 50", 50],
    ["r = 100 — a missed complaint costs a hundred false alarms", 100]
  ]),
  { value: 25, label: "cost ratio" }
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
costPlot = {
  const row = costRows.find(d => d.r === costRatio);
  const bars = [
    {policy: "flag nothing", cost: row.none, kind: "trivial"},
    {policy: "flag everything", cost: row.all, kind: "trivial"},
    {policy: "Elkan q* on raw scores", cost: row.raw, kind: "bad"},
    {policy: "Elkan q* on calibrated scores", cost: row.cal, kind: "good"},
    {policy: "threshold swept on cal", cost: row.swept, kind: "good"},
    {policy: "oracle — swept on test itself", cost: row.oracle, kind: "oracle"}
  ];
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 700,
    height: 300,
    marginLeft: 210,
    marginBottom: 50,
    x: { label: `total cost on the 10,000-document test set, in units of one false alarm — q* = ${row.qstar.toFixed(4)}`,
         grid: true },
    y: { label: null, domain: bars.map(d => d.policy) },
    color: { domain: ["trivial", "bad", "good", "oracle"],
             range: ["currentColor", "#B3453E", "#0E7C7B", "#1F4E79"], legend: false },
    marks: [
      Plot.barX(bars, { y: "policy", x: "cost", fill: "kind", rx: 3,
        title: d => `${d.policy}\n${d.cost.toLocaleString()} cost units` }),
      Plot.text(bars, { y: "policy", x: "cost", text: d => d.cost.toLocaleString(),
        dx: 6, textAnchor: "start", fontWeight: 600 }),
      Plot.ruleX([row.oracle], { stroke: "#1F4E79", strokeDasharray: "4 3" })
    ]
  });
}
```

::: {.column-margin}
Step the ratio up from 1 to 100 and watch the red bar. At $r = 10$ the
raw-score policy is respectable, 8% over the best threshold; at every other
ratio below 50 it overspends by 17–26%. At $r = 50$ it costs 56% more than the best
threshold available. [Uncalibrated scores fail worst exactly where the stakes are
highest]{.hl}, because that is where $q^*$ moves into the part of the score range
the model has compressed.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
Note what happens at $r = 1$, where Elkan's threshold is the familiar 0.5. The
raw model flags 78 documents and misses 563 of 632 complaints. This is the same
pathology as the 58.24 macro-F1 in @sec-classification-imbalance, seen from the
cost side: at equal costs the textbook threshold is 0.5, and on an uncalibrated
imbalanced model 0.5 is nowhere near the right place to stand.
:::

Sweeping directly for the cost-minimising threshold on `cal` does about as well
as calibrating and then applying the formula — regret 1% to 6% against 1% to 7%.
That is a genuinely useful practical finding: if all you need is one operating
point for one fixed cost ratio, you can skip calibration and sweep. Calibration
earns its place when the costs might change, when the number is shown to a
person, or when something downstream multiplies it.

For scale, the two trivial policies: flagging nothing costs $632r$, so 63,200 at
$r=100$; flagging everything costs 9,368 regardless of $r$. At $r = 100$ the raw
model's 8,373 is barely better than flagging the entire corpus.

## Zero-shot and few-shot with LLMs {#sec-classification-llm}

Everything so far assumed you have labels. Most projects start with none. The
question this section answers with measurements is what a general-purpose model
scores when you simply *ask* it, and — the part that decides real projects — how
that compares to a fine-tuned encoder at each label budget you might plausibly
have.

[**Zero-shot classification**](#gloss-zero-shot-classification){#term-zero-shot-classification .term-ref}
is attractive for an obvious reason: the labelling budget is zero and the model
ships today. It is also the setting in which every tool this chapter has built
stops working, which is the less obvious reason to read the numbers carefully.

One correction to that first sentence, which this section is itself evidence
for. The labelling budget for *training* is zero. The budget for finding out
whether it works is not: every number below rests on 2,000 labelled documents,
and you will need your own.

::: {#gloss-zero-shot-classification .column-margin .term-gloss}
**zero-shot classification** — labelling from an instruction alone, with no
examples and no training. The model returns a *word*, not a score, so there is
no threshold to move and no calibration map to fit. Every technique in
@sec-classification-imbalance, @sec-classification-calibration and
@sec-classification-costs needs a number between 0 and 1 that this setting does
not give you. [↩](#term-zero-shot-classification){.term-back}
:::

### Making the comparison honest

A comparison between a prompted model and a fine-tuned one is worthless unless
both are scored on the same documents. Prompting 10,000 reviews through a 27B
model is between 1.6 and 2.4 hours per condition depending on how busy the
laptop is — the lower figure from the median, the higher from the wall clock we
actually observed — so the LLM runs use a
*stratified 2,000-document subsample* of the same `test` slice — 1,874 satisfied
and 126 complaints, a 6.30% minority rate against the full slice's 6.32%.

The rule that makes this legitimate is that everything else gets re-scored on
that identical subsample. The tf-idf and BERTurk numbers in this section are not
the numbers from earlier sections; they are the same models read on the same
2,000 documents the LLMs saw, in the same order.

```text
re-scored on the 2,000-document subsample     acc   macro-F1  95% CI

always "satisfied"                           93.70    48.37
tf-idf + LR, class-weighted                  93.40    78.20   [74.77, 81.36]
tf-idf + LR, threshold moved to 0.166        95.40    80.23   [76.35, 83.60]
BERTurk fine-tuned,    200 labels            92.25    52.65   [49.77, 55.93]
BERTurk fine-tuned,    500 labels            93.70    59.47   [55.04, 63.97]
BERTurk fine-tuned,  1,000 labels            94.95    72.78   [68.12, 77.02]
BERTurk fine-tuned,  2,000 labels            96.05    82.00   [78.13, 85.42]
BERTurk fine-tuned,  5,000 labels            95.35    81.21   [77.57, 84.51]
BERTurk fine-tuned, 10,000 labels            96.65    84.97   [81.40, 88.07]
BERTurk fine-tuned, 20,000 labels            96.50    84.84   [81.21, 87.94]
BERTurk fine-tuned, 40,000 labels            96.85    86.81   [83.42, 89.60]
```

These are *not* the numbers in @sec-classification-baseline and
@sec-classification-finetune, and they should not be. Those were read on the
full 10,000; these are the same fitted models read on 2,000 of them. BERTurk at
500 labels scores 59.47 here and 56.46 there — same model, different slice.
[Any figure quoted in these two sections carries the subsample with it]{.hl}, so
never compare one against a number from earlier in the chapter.

Note that the majority-class baseline is 93.70% accuracy here. Any accuracy
figure in this section that starts with a 9 should be read against that number
and not against your intuitions.

::: {.column-margin}
The intervals are 2,000-resample bootstraps over the 2,000 documents. They are
wide — roughly ±3.5 points — because 126 complaints is not many, and the
minority class is what macro-F1 is mostly measuring. [A subsample buys you
affordable LLM runs and pays for it in resolution]{.hl}, and the honest response
is to print the interval rather than to pretend the point estimate is the
finding.
:::

Four models ran, all 4-bit quantised (`Q4_K_M`) on one laptop through `ollama`,
which is worth stating plainly: these are not frontier models behind an API.
They are what fits on a machine you can carry.

| model | parameters | on disk | note |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|
| `llama3.2:3b` | 3.2B | 2.0 GB | the small-model end of the range; **no thinking mode**, which is why it is the control in the `think: false` check |
| `qwen3.5:9b` | 9.7B | 6.6 GB | dense, the workhorse — **and a reasoning model**, which the broken run below is entirely about |
| `gemma3:27b` | 27.4B | 17.4 GB | dense, the largest here |
| `qwen3.6:35b-a3b` | 36.0B total, ~3B active | 23.9 GB | mixture-of-experts (@sec-moe), **also a reasoning model** |

: The four local models, all `Q4_K_M` quantised {tbl-colwidths="[30,22,16,32]"}

::: {.column-margin}
**4-bit quantised** means most weights are stored in four bits instead of
sixteen. `Q4_K_M` keeps some tensors at higher precision and stores a scale per
small block of weights, so the average is closer to five bits: `gemma3:27b`'s
27.4B weights take 17.4 GB, about a third of the 55 GB they would need at 16
bits. The cost in fidelity is usually small and is never zero. It is why a 27B model fits on a laptop at all. It also means
this comparison is not quite fair to the prompted side: BERTurk ran at full
precision and these did not. We could not measure the unquantised versions
because they do not fit on the machine, so [read the crossover as measured for
models you can run locally]{.hl}, and expect a full-precision or hosted model to
push it to the right.
:::

### The run that scored 93.75% by being completely broken

Before any results, the failure that nearly got published, because it is the
most useful thing in this section.

The first pass of this matrix scored `qwen3.5:9b` at 93.75% accuracy and 48.39
macro-F1 over the 400 documents it got through before it was killed. Read those
two numbers against the table above: 93.70 and 48.37. The model was predicting
"satisfied" on every single document, and the score it earned for that is the
majority-class baseline to within a rounding error.

Here is one archived record from that run, verbatim, and all 400 look like it:

```text
{"i": 0, "y": 1, "pred": 1, "conf": null, "ok": false, "raw": "",
 "secs": 2.408, "eval_count": 24, "prompt_eval_count": 99}

           raw : ''    <- what the parser reads. Empty, on all 400.
    eval_count : 24    <- tokens generated: exactly the cap, on all 400.
    parse rate : 0.0%  <- the field nobody was looking at.
```

`qwen3.5` is a reasoning model. `ollama` returns its chain of thought in a
separate `thinking` field, and the `response` field stays empty until the
thinking finishes. With `num_predict` capped at 24 tokens the budget was spent
entirely inside the reasoning block, `response` was never written, every answer
failed to parse, and [every document fell through to the fallback
label]{.hl} — which is the majority class, which is why the result looked
plausible instead of looking like a crash.

Note what the archived record does *not* contain: any sign of the thinking
field, or the reason generation stopped. The harness was not recording them,
which is why the diagnosis needed a fresh query to the model rather than a look
at the log. `think_chars` and `done_reason` are in the schema now — added
*because* of this, which is the usual way a log field gets born.

An accuracy of 93.75% on this corpus is not a result. It is the shape a broken
harness takes when the fallback is the majority class. Six of the ten runs in
this matrix would have carried the same defect.

Three changes fixed it, and only the first is about the bug:

1. Send `think: false`, with a fallback that retries without the field for models
   that reject it. Parse rate went from 0.0% to 100.0%, and the output on
   `llama3.2:3b` — which has no thinking mode — was byte-identical, confirming
   the flag is a no-op where it should be.
2. Abort a run whose first 40 answers parse below 50%, rather than spending nine
   hours of GPU time producing a table of majority-class baselines.
3. Smoke-test all six model/condition combinations on 24 documents each before
   committing the machine to an overnight queue.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**The rule those three fixes do not state, and should.** All three are specific
to this incident: one is a bug fix, two are sentries. The general rule is
simpler and it is the one to carry away — **an unparseable answer is not a
prediction.** Never let it fall through to a label: not to the majority class,
not to a random class, not to the previous document's answer. Emit a third
outcome, `unparseable`, and carry it into every metric you report: accuracy over
the documents that parsed, and the parse rate, side by side. A model that
answers 60% of the time at 95% accuracy is a different product from one that
answers every time at 57%. Score both over all documents with non-answers
counted as wrong and they look identical, 57% each; give the first a
majority-class fallback on this corpus and it scores about 94% and looks like
the better model. Only the pair of numbers tells them apart.
Note that the abort guard alone would not have saved us: a run parsing at 55%
passes it and still quietly imputes the majority class on the other 45%. Log the
raw response, the finish reason and the length of the reasoning field on every
call, because the field you need for the diagnosis is always the one you did not
think to record.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
This is the same lesson as the 27× inference outlier in
@sec-classification-finetune, arriving from the opposite direction. There the
number was implausibly *bad* and the harness was at fault. Here the number was
comfortably *good* and the harness was at fault. [The bad number gets
investigated; the good one gets published.]{.hl} That asymmetry, not the bug, is
the thing to design against — which is what the abort guard does.
:::

Every run reported below parsed at 100.0%.

### The results

Four models, three prompt settings, one corpus. The interesting comparison is
not which model wins — it is how much of the spread is explained by size, and
how much by things that cost nothing.

```text
2,000 documents, temperature 0, seed 42, single process. Every run parsed 100%.
                             acc  macroF1   95% CI       cP     cR    cF1   s/doc  prompt
                                                                                    tokens
llama3.2:3b      zero/tr   66.35    52.32  [50.10,54.68]  15.34  96.03  26.45  0.121   140
llama3.2:3b      zero/en   87.80    69.21  [65.98,72.38]  31.56  80.16  45.29  0.124   123
gemma3:27b       zero/tr   88.65    72.28  [69.18,75.28]  35.01  93.65  50.97  0.592   124
qwen3.5:9b       conf/tr   92.95    78.10  [74.85,81.25]  46.70  84.13  60.06  0.475   188
gemma3:27b        few/tr   93.20    79.45  [76.26,82.51]  47.90  90.48  62.64  0.560   549
qwen3.5:9b       zero/tr   93.70    79.53  [76.18,82.67]  50.00  83.33  62.50  0.365   136
qwen3.5:9b       zero/en   93.65    80.07  [76.88,83.18]  49.78  88.10  63.61  0.357   113
```

The widget below is the same table, sorted and plotted. Everything it shows is

Two boundaries worth naming before the findings. @sec-prompting takes prompt
design seriously as a subject; this section only asks what prompting *scores*
against a trained alternative. And @sec-decoding treats "getting a parseable
answer out of a model" as a problem in its own right — which, as the previous
subsection showed, it emphatically is.
