
::: {.column-margin}
Switch to **complaint precision and recall**. The grey bar joining the two dots
is the gap between them, and every single run leans the same way: recall high,
precision low. The two dashed rules are BERTurk at 40,000 labels — 74.42
precision, 76.19 recall — which is the only model on the chart whose two dots
sit almost on top of each other.
:::

Three findings, each tested with a **paired** bootstrap on the identical 2,000
documents rather than by eyeballing whether the intervals above overlap.
Overlapping intervals are not a test: two models scored on the same documents
share most of their sampling noise, and the difference can be significant while
the marginal intervals overlap heavily. Every $p$ below is from 10,000 paired
resamples of the difference.

#### Writing the prompt in English helps — if the model is weak

```text
                        tr       en      difference        p
llama3.2:3b           52.32    69.21   +16.90 [+14.59, +19.13]   0.0000
qwen3.5:9b            79.53    80.07    +0.54 [ -1.14,  +2.25]   0.5382
```

The folklore says: write the instruction in English even when the data is
Turkish. On the 3B model that is worth **+16.90 macro-F1** and is about as
unambiguous as a measurement gets. On the 9B model the same change is
[+0.54 points, $[-1.14, +2.25]$]{.hl} — which is not a demonstration that the
effect is gone. It is a demonstration that *if* an effect remains, it is smaller
than about two and a half macro-F1 points. That is a useful bound and a weaker
statement than "noise", and the distinction is worth keeping: the same design
would also have failed to resolve a real two-point gain.

The Turkish-instruction failure on `llama3.2:3b` is not a subtle degradation. It
labels 96.03% of complaints correctly and reaches 15.34% precision doing it —
it is calling almost everything a complaint. The English instruction does not
teach it Turkish; it stops it from collapsing onto one label.

::: {.column-margin}
This is why "use English prompts" survives as advice. It was *true*, on the
models people first tried it on, and it is still true for small models like
the 3B above — but it is repeated long after it stopped buying much on the
stronger models people use now. The check costs one extra run. [Advice about
LLMs has a shelf life measured in model generations]{.hl}, and the only way to
know whether a rule still holds is to spend an hour re-measuring it on the model
you are actually going to ship.
:::

#### Eight examples help — if the model is weak

```text
                       zero      few     difference        p
gemma3:27b            72.28    79.45    +7.17 [ +5.35,  +9.04]   0.0000
qwen3.5:9b            79.53    80.75    +1.22 [ -1.15,  +3.60]   0.3222
qwen3.6:35b-a3b       81.56    82.08    +0.51 [ -1.51,  +2.48]   0.6164
```

Same shape as the language result.
[**In-context learning**](#gloss-in-context-learning){#term-in-context-learning .term-ref}
with 8 labelled examples — four of each class, drawn from `fit` so that no test
document is ever in a prompt — moves `gemma3:27b` by 7.17 points and the two
`qwen3` models by amounts their intervals cannot separate from zero. Read those
the same way as the language result: `qwen3.6:35b-a3b`'s $+0.51$ carries
$[-1.51, +2.48]$, so what the run establishes is a *ceiling* of about two and a
half points, not the absence of a gain.

::: {#gloss-in-context-learning .column-margin .term-gloss}
**in-context learning** — learning a task from examples placed in the prompt. No
weight is updated and nothing survives the call: the same eight examples are
re-sent, re-read and re-charged for every document you classify. That is the
cost structure, and it is the opposite of fine-tuning, which pays once and then
serves cheaply. [↩](#term-in-context-learning){.term-back}
:::

Two practical notes. First, those 8 examples cost 584 prompt tokens against 136,
which is a 4.3× larger prompt on every one of your documents forever. Second,
the ordering and choice of examples is itself a source of variance large enough
to swamp the effect — Zhao et al. showed accuracy moving from near chance to
near state-of-the-art on the same task with the same number of examples, just
reordered [@zhao2021calibrate]. We used one fixed, seeded selection, so the
+7.17 on `gemma3:27b` should be read as *one draw* from that distribution rather
than as the expected value of adding examples.

#### Every prompted run here was recall-biased, and there is no threshold to fix it with

This is the finding with the most operational consequence, and it is visible in
the widget above under **complaint precision and recall**:

```text
                              complaint P    complaint R
llama3.2:3b zero/tr              15.34          96.03
gemma3:27b zero/tr               35.01          93.65
qwen3.5:9b zero/tr               50.00          83.33
qwen3.6:35b-a3b few/tr           56.98          80.95
BERTurk, 40,000 labels           74.42          76.19
```

Every prompted run flags far more complaints than it should. The best of them
reaches 56.98% precision at 80.95% recall; BERTurk sits at 74.42 and 76.19,
nearly balanced. Ask a model "is this a complaint?" and it says yes too often.

[The problem is not that the operating point is wrong. It is that there is no
operating point to move.]{.hl} @sec-classification-imbalance fixed the mirror
image of this pathology — a linear model that flagged far *too few* complaints at
0.5 — by shifting one threshold, and gained 19.42 macro-F1 points for free. That instrument does not exist here. A zero-shot model returns
the *word* `ŞİKAYET`, not a number, and you cannot threshold a word.

Everything this chapter built downstream of a score goes with it: no ROC curve,
no PR curve, no isotonic calibration, no $q^*$ from a cost ratio, no
cost-minimising sweep. You can recover some of it — read the model's own
log-probabilities for the two candidate answer words, `ŞİKAYET` against
`MEMNUN`, if your serving software exposes them, which turns a word back into a
score; or ask for a confidence in words, as the next subsection does. But by
default, choosing a prompted model means choosing to give up the threshold.

One boundary on this finding: we did not try to argue the models out of it. A
prompt that says "answer `ŞİKAYET` only if the reviewer states a concrete fault"
would plausibly move the operating point, and we did not measure that. What no
prompt gives you is a *dial* — a knob you can turn after deployment, when the
cost ratio changes and you need a different point on the same curve.

#### Is a confidence the model writes down a probability?

The `conf` condition asked `qwen3.5:9b` for `LABEL|CONFIDENCE`, a 0–100 integer.
All 2,000 answers parsed. This is
[**verbalised confidence**](#gloss-verbalised-confidence){#term-verbalised-confidence .term-ref},
and it is the closest thing to a score the zero-shot setting offers.

::: {#gloss-verbalised-confidence .column-margin .term-gloss}
**verbalised confidence** — a number the model writes out as text, rather than a
probability read off its scores. Judge it the way
@sec-classification-calibration judges any other confidence: does it match the
frequency of being right, and does it separate right from wrong?
[↩](#term-verbalised-confidence){.term-back}
:::

```text
stated confidence      n      actually right
     50                3          100.0%
     60                1          100.0%
     70                1          100.0%
     75               62           80.6%
     85               25           76.0%
     90              286           83.2%
     92               23           82.6%
     95            1,549           95.4%
    100               50          100.0%

mean stated confidence  93.53      overall accuracy  92.95      gap  +0.58
expected calibration error (over stated values)                 1.80
```

On the test people actually report — does average stated confidence match
average accuracy? — it does remarkably well. The average stated confidence is
93.53% and the model is right 92.95% of the time, a gap of **+0.58 points**.
Binned over the nine stated values its ECE is **1.80**, against 8.98 for the
class-weighted tf-idf model. Read that comparison loosely: as
@sec-classification-calibration insisted, an ECE means nothing without its
binning scheme, and this one uses nine bins the *model* chose rather than
fifteen equal-width ones. It is the right order of magnitude, not a like-for-like
number. Lin et al. showed that a model can be trained to express calibrated
uncertainty in words [@lin2022teaching], and on this task, out of the box, it
is.

Then look at the second column. **1,549 of the 2,000 documents — 77.45% — got
the same number, 95.** There are 9 distinct values in the entire run. A confidence that
is almost always 95 cannot tell you much about which documents to route to a
human.

Measured as a detector of its own errors, stated confidence scores an
[AUROC of 0.667]{.hl}. BERTurk's own top-label probability, on the same 2,000
documents, scores **0.843** across 1,325 distinct values. Both models are
somewhat able to flag their own mistakes; the trained one is better at it and
gives you a dial rather than a switch.

Read that gap with one caveat, because the chapter has already told you the
reason and not drawn the consequence. AUROC awards half credit on ties, and
77.45% of the LLM's documents share a single confidence value — so roughly
three-fifths of all document pairs are ties for it. Of the pairs AUROC actually
compares, one right answer against one wrong answer, 45% are ties; for
BERTurk, with 1,325 distinct values, almost none are.
Part of 0.667-against-0.843 is a worse signal and part of it is a *coarser* one,
and this comparison does not separate them. The practical conclusion survives
either way — nine values give you a switch, 1,325 give you a dial — but do not
read the gap as "the LLM's confidence is 0.18 of AUROC worse".

The one useful split is real, though: at stated confidence ≥ 95 the model is
right 95.56% of the time (n = 1,599), and below 95 it is right 82.54%
(n = 401). If your workflow only needs "send a fifth of these to a person", that
is enough to build on — with the caveat the rest of this chapter would insist
on. We picked 95 by looking at that table, and that table is the evaluation set.
By the rule stated in @sec-classification-setup, [95.56 against 82.54 is
therefore an **oracle** split and an upper bound]{.hl}, not a result. Choose the
cut on held-out documents before you route anything on it.

::: {.column-margin}
Xiong et al. evaluated black-box confidence elicitation across models and tasks
and report AUROCs in the 0.522–0.605 band, together with a systematic tendency
to overconfidence they attribute to models imitating how people express
certainty [@xiong2024llmsexpress]. Our 0.667 is slightly above their range and
our *average* gap is small — but the 77.5%-at-one-value concentration is
precisely the failure mode they describe. [A confidence can be right on average
and still separate almost nothing.]{.hl}
:::

## Small model vs. LLM: the crossover {#sec-classification-crossover}

Now the decision. Both previous sections produced a number on the same 2,000
documents, so they can finally be compared directly. Two axes decide it, and
neither is quality-versus-quality: **how many labels do you have**, and **what
does a document cost to classify**.

### The crossover is at 2,000 labels, and it is a tie rather than a win

So where do the two curves meet? The honest way to answer is not to compare
two point estimates, because two numbers that differ can still be the same
number wearing noise. Both systems ran on the same documents, so we can pair
them and bootstrap the difference directly.

```text
paired bootstrap, same 2,000 documents, 10,000 resamples

BERTurk  1,000 labels  vs  qwen3.6:35b-a3b zero-shot    -8.79 [-13.53,  -4.24]   p = 0.0002
BERTurk  2,000 labels  vs  qwen3.6:35b-a3b zero-shot    +0.43 [ -3.17,  +3.85]   p = 0.8030
BERTurk  2,000 labels  vs  qwen3.6:35b-a3b 8-shot       -0.08 [ -3.78,  +3.61]   p = 0.9728
BERTurk 40,000 labels  vs  qwen3.6:35b-a3b 8-shot       +4.73 [ +1.56,  +7.90]   p = 0.0028
```

[At 2,000 labels the fine-tuned encoder and the best prompted model are
**statistically indistinguishable at this sample size**.]{.hl} That is a weaker
claim than a tie, and the interval says how much weaker. With 126 complaints in
the subsample the paired standard error is 1.89 macro-F1 points, so this design
can only rule out differences larger than about **3.2 points** (the 90% interval
runs $[-3.18, +3.02]$, which is what an equivalence test would work with) and
has 80% power only against differences above **5.3 points**. Read the 2,000-label
row as *we could not tell them apart*, not as *they are the same*: a genuine
equivalence claim at, say, ±1 point would need roughly ten times this many
documents at this class balance. Note also that our own +4.73 at 40,000 labels
sits *below* that 80%-power threshold — it reached significance, but the design
was not built to guarantee it would.

At 1,000 labels the LLM wins by 8.79 points and the result is not close. At
40,000 the encoder wins by 4.73 and that result is not close either.

So the crossover on this task sits at roughly **2,000 labelled documents**, and
the useful way to hold it is as three regimes rather than a verdict — plus a
fourth option that the "prompt or fine-tune" framing hides:

- **Under ~1,000 labels.** Prompt. The encoder has not yet learned what a
  complaint is — at 500 labels it scores 59.47 macro-F1 on this subsample
  against the majority baseline's 48.37, catching 14.29% of complaints — and no
  *learning-rate sweep* changes that. A different recipe might: `setfit` (@sec-classification-tools)
  is contrastive fine-tuning of a sentence encoder
  plus a logistic head, it is built for exactly this budget, and it routinely
  reports usable macro-F1 from 8–64 examples per class
  [@tunstall2022setfit]. We did not measure it, and running it at 200, 500 and
  1,000 labels is the single measurement most likely to change this bullet.
- **Around 2,000.** Genuinely a coin flip on quality. Decide on cost, latency,
  operational control, and whether you need a threshold. All four of those point
  the same way, which is the subject of the next subsection.
- **Above 2,000.** Fine-tune. We have exactly one more measured point — at
  40,000 the encoder wins by 4.73 — so *where* between 2,000 and 40,000 the gap
  becomes decisive is interpolation from the encoder's own learning curve, not a
  measurement. What is measured is the direction, and that the encoder is the
  only one of the two that hands you a score.
- **The option this framing leaves out.** You do not have to choose between
  paying the prompted model forever and labelling by hand. Spend it *once*:
  label your unlabelled pool with the big model, then fine-tune the encoder on
  those labels — the LLM as annotator, the encoder as student
  [@hsieh2023distilling; @gilardi2023chatgpt]. Our own numbers price it. At
  352.6 seconds per thousand documents, labelling all 40,000 is under four hours
  of laptop GPU, and what it buys is a student that serves **142× cheaper** *and*
  hands back the score, the ROC curve and the threshold that
  @sec-classification-llm showed prompting takes away. The labels are noisy,
  so the natural reference point is the teacher's 81.56 rather than a human
  annotator's. A student trained on a teacher's labels can land below the
  teacher or, as @hsieh2023distilling report, above it; where this one lands is
  exactly the measurement we did not make, and it is the one we would make
  first.

This is consistent with the published picture rather than a contradiction of it.
Edwards and Camacho-Collados found fine-tuning ahead by 0.119 micro-F1 with full
training data across 16 datasets but prompting ahead outright in the one-shot
regime [@edwards2024incontext]; Bucher and Martini put the crossover above
roughly 200 training observations, though against zero-shot BART-large-MNLI
rather than a modern instruction-tuned model [@bucher2024finetuned]. Our
crossover is an order of magnitude higher than theirs, which is what you would
expect when the prompted model is a 2026 36B mixture-of-experts rather than a
2019 entailment model. [The crossover is a property of the pair you are
comparing, not a constant]{.hl} — which is the argument for measuring it on your
own task rather than citing anyone's number, including ours.

### What a document costs

Quality is where the argument starts. Cost is where it usually ends.

```text
option                              docs/sec    seconds per 1,000 docs

tf-idf + LR, batched                  72,972              0.014
tf-idf + LR, one at a time             6,543              0.153
BERTurk fine-tuned, batched              470              2.128
llama3.2:3b  zero-shot, one at a time      8.3           121.0
qwen3.5:9b  8-shot, one at a time          3.4           289.9
qwen3.6:35b-a3b  8-shot, one at a time     3.3           301.5
qwen3.6:35b-a3b  zero-shot, one at a time  2.8           352.6
qwen3.5:9b  zero-shot, one at a time       2.7           365.0
gemma3:27b  8-shot, one at a time          1.8           559.8
gemma3:27b  zero-shot, one at a time       1.7           592.5
```

Read the right-hand column as a ratio and the argument stops being close.
[Classifying a million documents costs 14 seconds with the vectoriser, 35
minutes with the fine-tuned encoder, and three and a half days with the best
prompted model.]{.hl} The encoder is **142× cheaper per document** than the
prompted model it ties with at 2,000 labels; the vectoriser is roughly
**22,000× cheaper**.

Two things that ratio is and is not. It is a batched encoder against a
single-stream local server, which is the comparison most small teams actually
face. It is *not* the most favourable arrangement for the prompted side: the
table's own tf-idf pair shows batching alone is worth 11× (72,972 against
6,543), and a hosted API batching properly would recover a good part of that.
What batching cannot recover is the mechanism underneath. The encoder reads a
document once and emits a number. The prompted model must write its answer one
token at a time, and every token costs a full pass through a network thirty to
three hundred times larger. [Batching amortises the overhead; it does not change
the arithmetic.]{.hl}

::: {.column-margin}
One row of that table should stop you: **8-shot is faster than zero-shot in all
three pairs it can be compared in** — 301.5 against 352.6 on `qwen3.6`, 289.9
against 365.0 on `qwen3.5`, 559.8 against 592.5 on `gemma3` — despite a prompt
4.3× longer.

Part of it is straightforward. Latency tracks *output* tokens, generated one at
a time, not prompt tokens, processed in parallel. The `conf` run generates 7.1
tokens against 4.1 and is duly the slowest `qwen3.5` condition.

But that does not close the case. `qwen3.5` zero and few both generate 4.1
tokens, so output length cannot explain *this* pair.

The likely remainder is that the 8-shot prefix is identical across all 2,000
requests and the server caches it. [We did not measure that, so we are not
claiming it]{.hl} — and on a laptop this noisy, a 20% gap between two runs made
at different times is not something to build an argument on.
:::

Every LLM figure is a **median**, and that choice is not cosmetic. The `qwen3.5:9b`
zero-shot run has a mean of 3.371 seconds per document against a median of
0.365 — a 9× discrepancy produced by 18 documents that stalled, the worst for
980 seconds. Those stalls are a property of a laptop that decided to do
something else for a while, not of the model. Quoting the mean would have
inflated this model's cost by an order of magnitude. That would have made the
comparison above meaningless, and it would have been unfair *to* this model,
not in its favour.

::: {.column-margin}
Note where the mixture-of-experts model lands. `qwen3.6:35b-a3b` has 36B
parameters but activates about 3B per token, and it serves a document in 0.353s
— *faster* than the dense 9.7B model at 0.365s and 1.7× faster than the dense
27.4B at 0.592s, while scoring higher than both. This is
@sec-moe's argument arriving as a serving bill: [what you pay for
at inference is active parameters, not total ones]{.hl}.
:::

There is a second asymmetry, and it runs the other way. The prompted models pay
per document forever, while the encoder pays once: the 2,000-label model that
ties with the best prompt is 1,260 optimiser steps, about **6.5 minutes** of
corrected GPU time, repaid after roughly **1,300 documents**.

But 6.5 minutes is the *GPU* bill, and it is the smaller half. The encoder also
needs 2,000 labelled documents; the 8-shot prompt needs eight. This chapter
cannot price your labelling — at ten seconds a document that is five and a half
hours of somebody's attention, and at a minute a document it is a working week.
[The GPU bill is repaid in a morning. The labels are the real cost, and they are
the reason @sec-classification-finetune calls labelling the bottleneck.]{.hl}
What the labels buy is the right to be in this comparison at all.

### The decision, on the two axes that decide it

Enough measurements. What a reader actually needs is not the scoreboard but a
way to locate their own situation on it — so put your label count and your
document volume in, and read off which system the numbers point to.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
crossRows = [
  {name: "tf-idf + LR, threshold moved", mf1: 80.23, s1k: 0.014, kind: "trained", labels: 40000},
  {name: "BERTurk, 1,000 labels",     mf1: 72.78, s1k: 2.128, kind: "trained", labels: 1000},
  {name: "BERTurk, 2,000 labels",     mf1: 82.00, s1k: 2.128, kind: "trained", labels: 2000},
  {name: "BERTurk, 40,000 labels",    mf1: 86.81, s1k: 2.128, kind: "trained", labels: 40000},
  {name: "llama3.2:3b zero/tr",       mf1: 52.32, s1k: 121.0, kind: "llm", labels: 0},
  {name: "llama3.2:3b zero/en",       mf1: 69.21, s1k: 124.0, kind: "llm", labels: 0},
  {name: "qwen3.5:9b zero/tr",        mf1: 79.53, s1k: 365.0, kind: "llm", labels: 0},
  {name: "qwen3.5:9b few/tr",         mf1: 80.75, s1k: 289.9, kind: "llm", labels: 8},
  {name: "gemma3:27b zero/tr",        mf1: 72.28, s1k: 592.5, kind: "llm", labels: 0},
  {name: "gemma3:27b few/tr",         mf1: 79.45, s1k: 559.8, kind: "llm", labels: 8},
  {name: "qwen3.6:35b-a3b zero/tr",   mf1: 81.56, s1k: 352.6, kind: "llm", labels: 0},
  {name: "qwen3.6:35b-a3b few/tr",    mf1: 82.08, s1k: 301.5, kind: "llm", labels: 8}
]
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
crossPlot = Plot.plot({
  width: 700,
  height: 420,
  marginLeft: 62,
  marginBottom: 52,
  marginRight: 20,
  x: {label: "seconds to classify 1,000 documents  (log scale, lower is better)",
      type: "log", grid: true,
      ticks: [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000],
      tickFormat: d => d < 1 ? String(d) : d.toLocaleString()},
  y: {label: "macro-F1 on the 2,000-document subsample", domain: [40, 95], grid: true},
  color: {domain: ["trained", "llm"],
          range: ["#1F4E79", "#B3453E"],
          legend: true,
          tickFormat: d => ({trained: "trained on labels",
                             llm: "prompted, no training"})[d]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([48.37], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.text([{x: 0.02, y: 48.37}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: ["always “satisfied” — 48.37"],
      dy: -8, fill: "currentColor", textAnchor: "start", fontSize: 9}),
    Plot.dot(crossRows, {x: "s1k", y: "mf1", fill: "kind", r: 6,
      title: d => `${d.name}\nmacro-F1 ${d.mf1.toFixed(2)}\n${d.s1k}s per 1,000 documents`
                + `\n${d.labels.toLocaleString()} labels used`}),
    Plot.text(crossRows, {x: "s1k", y: "mf1", text: "name", dy: -12,
      fontSize: 9, textAnchor: "middle"})
  ]

```

::: {.column-margin}
Down and to the right is worse on both axes at once. Everything trained sits in
the left half of the chart by two to four orders of magnitude; everything
prompted sits in the right. [The best prompted model (82.08) and BERTurk at
2,000 labels (82.00) are at the same height and 142× apart
horizontally]{.hl} — which is the whole argument of this section in one pair of
dots. Both coordinates of every point are in the two `text` tables above, so the
chart adds convenience rather than information.
:::

### The two models fail on different documents

@sec-classification-errors will cross-tabulate tf-idf against BERTurk document
by document and find they miss different ones; that non-overlap is the condition
under which combining two models could help. Here is the same cross-tabulation
for `qwen3.6:35b-a3b` 8-shot against BERTurk at 40,000 labels, on the shared
2,000:

```text
                          BERTurk right    BERTurk wrong
LLM right                     1,871              28
LLM wrong                        66              35

they agree on 95.30% of documents
an oracle picking the better of the two per document: 92.62 macro-F1
BERTurk alone:                                       86.81
```

The 28 documents in the top-right corner are real: they are cases the fine-tuned
encoder gets wrong and the prompted model gets right. An oracle that could always
pick the winner would score 92.62 against BERTurk's 86.81 — **5.81 points on the
table**.

We are not shipping that, and the reason is the point of this section rather
than a footnote. To capture those 28 documents you would have to send documents
to the LLM, and the LLM costs 142× more per document. A router that scores
everything with BERTurk and forwards even 10% of traffic to the prompted model
runs at 32.3 seconds per 1,000 documents against 2.1 — **15× the serving bill**
to chase 28 documents in 2,000.
[The 5.81 points are real and the mechanism to collect them is unaffordable]{.hl},
which is the honest shape of most ensemble opportunities: visible in an offline
cross-tabulation, deleted by the cost column.

The version that *does* pay is the one the confidence measurement above points
at: use the cheap model's own score, which has AUROC 0.843 against its own
errors, to route the uncertain tail to a person rather than to a bigger model.
That is @sec-classification-costs's machinery, applied to a different decision,
and it needs no second model at all.

## Error analysis as a discipline {#sec-classification-errors}

Every number so far tells you *how often* a model is wrong. None of them tells
you *what* it is wrong about, and that is the question that decides whether you
ship. This section is the habit: after the metrics, read the mistakes.

We compare the two *trained* models at the operating points already chosen —
tf-idf at $t = 0.166$ on the complaint side, and BERTurk at 40,000 labels read
at $0.5$. On the 10,000-document test
set that is 373 complaints caught out of 632 for tf-idf against 452 for BERTurk,
at 57.38% and 72.32% precision.

### The 2×2 nobody builds, and should

At these two operating points the aggregate delta is 7.35 macro-F1 points —
85.02 for BERTurk against 77.66 for the re-thresholded vectoriser — and that
single number hides a trade. The only way to see the trade is to cross-tabulate
the two models document by document.

:::: {.anlp-fig}
```{=html}

  <text x="284" y="188" class="t-mid t-b t-mono t-accent">332</text>
  <text x="284" y="206" class="t-xs t-mid t-muted">3.32% &#183; 122 of them complaints</text>

  <rect x="448" y="132" width="296" height="86" rx="6" class="box-warm"/>
  <text x="592" y="164" class="t-mid t-b t-warm">neither model reaches</text>
  <text x="592" y="188" class="t-mid t-b t-mono t-warm">204</text>
  <text x="592" y="206" class="t-xs t-mid t-muted">2.04% &#183; 137 of them complaints</text>

  <line x1="136" y1="238" x2="744" y2="238" class="ln-thin"/>
  <text x="136" y="258" class="t-sm">net <tspan class="t-b t-mono">332 &#8722; 149 = 183</tspan> documents &#8212; 1.83 accuracy points, 7.35 macro-F1 points</text>
  <text x="136" y="278" class="t-sm t-muted">the 137 complaints in the bottom-right cell are <tspan class="t-b">21.7% of every complaint on the test set</tspan></text>
  <text x="136" y="294" class="t-xs t-muted">tf-idf read at t = 0.166 on the complaint side; BERTurk (40,000 labels) read at 0.5</text>
</svg>
```
::: {.fig-cap}
The 7.35-point headline is a net figure. Switching models fixes 332 documents
and breaks 149 — a real gain, but 45% of the gross gain is handed back
(149/332), leaving a net 183. If those 149
happen to be your highest-value cases, the aggregate number is lying to you.
:::
::::

Three things fall out of that grid that the leaderboard cannot show you.

**The gain is smaller than it looks, and it is a trade.** 332 documents get
fixed; 149 that tf-idf handled break. [Nobody who reports a 7.35-point
improvement is lying, but nobody who reports it is telling you that they broke
149 documents either.]{.hl} If your complaints route to a human queue and 149 of
them were the ones that queue was tuned around, the "upgrade" is a regression
for that team.

**There is a hard floor, and it is high.** 204 documents defeat both models, and
137 of them are complaints — [21.7% of every complaint in the test set is missed
by a sparse linear model and a fine-tuned transformer alike]{.hl}. That is not a
capacity problem you fix with a bigger encoder. It is either genuinely
ambiguous text or a broken label, and the next two subsections argue it is
mostly the second.

**The two models fail on different things.** 685 documents are missed by at
least one of the two models, and only 204 of those are missed by both; on the
other 481 the models disagree. That non-overlap is exactly the condition under which an
ensemble helps — and, more usefully here, it is the condition under which
*reading the disagreements* teaches you something, because each model's errors
have a shape.

::: {.column-margin}
The disagreement 2×2 costs one `numpy` line and takes five seconds. Build it
every single time you replace a model in production. The version that matters
most is not this one but the one restricted to the class you care about: 122
complaints gained, 43 lost.
:::

### Slice before you conclude

The second cheap habit: split the test set on anything you can measure without
labelling, and check whether the aggregate holds inside each slice. Document
length is free.

```text
length (chars)      n    complaints   tf-idf err   BERTurk err   ratio
<50             1,644         6.14%        5.29%         4.50%    1.18
50–99           2,253         6.39%        5.77%         3.99%    1.44
100–199         3,499         6.09%        4.86%         3.12%    1.56
200–399         2,096         7.16%        5.82%         3.10%    1.88
400+              508         4.72%        5.31%         2.95%    1.80
```

[tf-idf's error rate is flat.]{.hl} It moves between 4.86% and 5.82% with no
trend — a longer review gives a bag-of-words model more words, but it also gives
it more chances for a cheerful word to outvote the complaint. BERTurk's error
rate falls almost monotonically, from 4.50% on reviews under 50 characters to
3.10% on reviews of 200–399. The advantage is 1.18× on the shortest documents
and 1.88× on the second-longest bucket.

That is the encoder's actual selling point stated precisely: **it is not
uniformly better, it is better at long documents**, because that is where
negation, concession and scope live and where a bag of words has nothing to say
about any of them. If your production traffic is mostly one-line reviews, the
1.18× is the number you should be budgeting against, not the 1.88×.

::: {.column-margin}
Read the 400+ row with suspicion. It is 508 documents holding roughly 24
complaints, so BERTurk's 2.95% is about 15 errors. One document moves it by 0.2
points. The trend across the first four buckets is the finding; the last row is
consistent with it, not evidence for it.
:::

### Sort the errors by confidence, not at random

Reading a random sample of errors mostly teaches you that hard cases are hard.
Reading the errors the model was *most confident* about is where the information
is, because a model that is confidently wrong is usually being punished for
being right.

Here are BERTurk's most confident mistakes, glossed into English. The
probabilities are the model's, on the complaint side.

```text
gold        p(complaint)   review (glossed)
complaint         0.0011   "I chose it because the price was right, but I was
                            very pleased once I used it … definitely worth it."
complaint         0.0012   "Thank you so much, prettier than the picture, I
                            loved it, an anniversary gift for my wife :-)"
satisfied         0.9988   "It broke within two months and became unusable
                            (I'm giving five stars so my review shows up at the
                            top, normally it doesn't deserve a star)"
satisfied         0.9986   "The suction was weak and it burned out after 5–6
                            months."
satisfied         0.9986   "Friends, it does nothing for belly fat, that's
                            certain … so if you're buying it for your belly,
                            don't."
satisfied         0.9988   "You'll regret it if you don't buy it."
satisfied         0.9987   "A so-so product."
```

The third row is the one that needs no adjudication, and it is worth dwelling
on. **The reviewer states, in the review, that the star rating is strategic
rather than evaluative** — five stars so the complaint floats to the top of the
listing. Our labels are derived from star ratings. So the label is a faithful
record of the stars and a false record of the sentiment, and the reviewer has
helpfully documented the exact mechanism by which our ground truth fails.

The rows above and below it read the same way to us: a vacuum that burned out,
a product that "does nothing," a review that ends *don't buy it* — all filed as
satisfied. And in the other direction, two glowing reviews filed as complaints.
[We are stating that as our reading, not as a measurement]{.hl}: no independent
Turkish-speaking annotator has re-adjudicated these, so we will not put a number
on how many of the 204 shared failures are label errors. What we will say is
that the top of the confidence-sorted error list is dominated by cases where the
model looks more right than the label, which is exactly the diagnostic
@frenay2014classification describe and exactly what @sec-audit told you to go
looking for.

The last two rows are instructive in a different way. *"You'll regret it if you
don't buy it"* is a genuine model error: it contains every lexical marker of a
complaint — regret, negation, a warning — arranged to mean the opposite.
*"A so-so product"* is neither a model error nor a clear label error. It is a
shrug, and a shrug next to a five-star rating is a labelling convention, not a
language problem.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The rule this produces

Sort your errors by model confidence, descending, and read the first fifty by
hand. If most of them look like label errors, stop tuning the model — you are
now measuring your annotation process, and no architecture change will move the
number. Re-label instead, or change the labelling function.
:::

### What the encoder buys, in sentences

The 122 complaints BERTurk catches that tf-idf misses have a shape, and it is
not vocabulary. These are all documents where tf-idf scored well under its 0.166
threshold and BERTurk scored above 0.9:

```text
p_lin   p_bert   review (glossed)
0.135    0.9987  "After one month's use it snapped in the middle."
0.143    0.9976  "The reception isn't anything to write home about,
                  normal for the price."
0.152    0.9801  "The numbers on the parts are printed wrong; assembling
                  it into a whole is exhausting."
0.143    0.9976  "I put it downstairs in my duplex and it doesn't reach
                  upstairs; upstairs and it doesn't reach downstairs.
                  Very weak … I read the reviews and can't believe it's
                  the same modem."
```

None of these contain a complaint word in the sense a bag of words understands.
The first carries its entire meaning in one rare verb (*koptu*, "snapped"). The
second is a concessive: the complaint is in the first clause and the second
clause partly retracts it, which is a structure tf-idf cannot represent because
it has thrown away the order. The fourth is a complaint expressed as a
*narrative* — no evaluative vocabulary at all, just a description of the product
failing to do its job twice. [Sparse features need the word; the encoder needs
the sentence.]{.hl}

And the errors both models share, similarly glossed, fall into two families:

```text
"It drops out now and then, but it'll do."          lukewarm
"It'll do, for the money it's fine."                lukewarm
"A so-so product."                                  lukewarm
"You'll regret it if you don't buy it."             negated regret
"The hose looks low quality."                       hedged
"Downside:"                                         empty
```

The lukewarm family is the interesting one, because it is not really a modelling
failure. *İdare eder* — "it'll do" — is a shrug that Turkish reviewers routinely
pair with four or five stars, so the label says satisfied and the text says
neither. No classifier can recover a distinction the labels do not encode. The
last row is worse: a review whose entire text is the word *downside* followed by
a colon. It has a gold label. It contains no information. [Some fraction of
every test set is unlabelable, and it sets a ceiling you cannot see from the
metrics.]{.hl}

### The four habits

Everything above is four cheap things done in order, and they generalise to any
classifier you will ever ship:

1. **Cross-tabulate against the model you are replacing.** An aggregate
   improvement is a net figure. Find out what you broke.
2. **Slice on something free.** Length, source, date, product category, document
   language. Check that the win survives inside each slice before you claim it.
3. **Sort errors by confidence and read the top of the list.** Confident
   mistakes concentrate label errors; random samples concentrate genuine
   ambiguity.
4. **Separate your errors from the dataset's.** Ask of each mistake: could a
   careful human have got this right from the text alone? If the answer is no,
   it is not a model problem, and tuning will not fix it.

## Intuition checks {#sec-classification-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. All six are questions this chapter settled
with a measurement rather than an argument, so the answers carry numbers you can
check.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. A colleague reports 94.3% accuracy on this corpus. How impressed should you be?

Not at all, and you can say so before seeing anything else. A model that answers
"satisfied" to every input scores **93.68%** here, because that is the base rate.
94.3% is 0.6 points above a model with no features, no training and no
parameters.

The uncorrected baseline in @sec-classification-metrics scores exactly 94.28% at
$t = 0.5$ — and catches **69 of 632 complaints**. It is not a slightly-better-
than-nothing model; it is a nearly-nothing model wearing a respectable number.

The habit worth forming: before you look at any accuracy figure, compute the
majority-class rate and subtract. If the gap is small, ask for a different
metric. Matthews correlation is the cheapest honest replacement — it gives the
constant predictors exactly 0.000 and the random guessers values within 0.02 of
zero.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Your macro-F1 goes from 58.24 to 77.66 and the only change is one constant. Did you cheat?

No — provided you can show the ranking did not move, and provided the constant
was chosen on held-out data.

The proof is in @sec-classification-imbalance: average precision is 60.30 and
AUC is 93.24 *both* before and after. Those two statistics depend only on the
order the model puts documents in. They come out identical to four significant
figures because the model is byte-for-byte the same, and a ranking statistic
that did not move is the evidence you can show someone else; all that changed
is where we cut.

The cheat would be picking 0.166 by sweeping thresholds on the test set. That is
why every threshold in this chapter is chosen on the 8,000-document `cal` slice
and only then applied to test. The chapter does report test-swept thresholds —
labelled **oracle** — but only as an upper bound to measure regret against, never
as a result.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. You have 800 labels and two days. Fine-tune BERTurk or fit tf-idf?

At 800 labels this is genuinely close, and the honest answer is *fit tf-idf
first, today, and then decide*.

The measured curves bracket you. At 500 labels tf-idf scores **60.82** and
BERTurk **56.46** — the sparse model wins. At 1,000 labels tf-idf scores
**61.60** and BERTurk **71.57** — the encoder wins by ten points. Your 800 sits
inside a crossover that is steep on the encoder side and flat on the sparse side.

What tips it is the cost asymmetry, not the accuracy. The tf-idf fit takes about
a tenth of a second. If it lands where you need, you are finished before lunch.
If it does not, you have lost nothing and you now have a floor to beat and a
labelled set already loaded. [Run the cheap thing first not because it usually
wins, but because finding out costs nothing.]{.hl}

Now notice the option the question does not offer you.
@sec-classification-crossover measured a third answer near this budget, and it
needs its own evaluation set to be quoted honestly: on the shared 2,000-document
subsample a prompted 36B model scores **81.56** macro-F1 with *zero* labels,
against BERTurk's **72.78** at 1,000 labels on those same documents — the
paired bootstrap puts that gap at **8.79 points** in the prompt's favour. Fit
tf-idf anyway; it is a tenth of a second and it is your floor. But "which of
these two do I train" stopped being the whole question, and what should settle
it is the column the original answer never had: the prompt costs **352 seconds
per 1,000 documents** against the vectoriser's 0.014, and it gives you no
threshold to move.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Adding 500 labels made AUC go down. Should you roll back?

Look at what else moved first. Going from 500 to 1,000 labels, BERTurk's AUC
falls 83.00 → 82.76, and over the same step average precision rises 26.98 →
45.72 and macro-F1 rises 56.46 → 71.57.

That is not a contradiction, it is the two metrics measuring different regions.
The false-positive rate divides by 9,368 satisfied reviews, so mistakes among
the easy majority barely register; precision divides by however many documents
you actually flagged, which is a much smaller number [@davis2006relationship].
The extra labels improved the model exactly where the decision happens and
slightly disturbed a part of the ranking nobody operates in.

Roll back only if your product lives at low thresholds across the whole ranking.
Ours does not — nobody reads all 10,000 reviews — so ship it. The general rule:
on an imbalanced problem, quote **average precision against the base rate**
(here 60.30 against 6.32%, a 9.54× lift) and treat AUC as secondary.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Class weighting raised your F1. What did it cost?

Its calibration, and probably more than you wanted to pay.

`class_weight="balanced"` takes macro-F1 from 58.24 to 76.09 and takes expected
calibration error from **3.96 to 14.18** — a 3.6× increase. The reweighted
model's mean predicted probability is 0.795 against a true rate of 0.9368. It has
learned a prior that is not the prior of the world it will run in.

If the only thing you ever do with the output is `argmax`, this is free. It stops
being free the moment the number is displayed to a human ("87% likely a
complaint"), multiplied by a cost, fed to a downstream rule, or compared across
model versions. And note that you did not have to pay it at all: moving the
threshold on the *unweighted* model reaches 77.66 — better than class weighting
— with ECE untouched at 3.96.

Van den Goorbergh and colleagues found the same trade on clinical risk models
and argued it is rarely worth making [@vandengoorbergh2022harm].
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. You applied the textbook cost-optimal threshold and the review queue exploded. What went wrong?

The formula is almost certainly fine. The input to it was not a probability.

Elkan's $q^* = C_{FP}/(C_{FN}+C_{FP})$ is correct, and it assumes $q$ is a
calibrated probability [@elkan2001foundations]. At a cost ratio of 100 that
threshold is 0.0099. Feed it raw logistic-regression scores and the model flags
8,073 of 9,368 satisfied reviews, because its scores are compressed into a band
where 0.0099 catches nearly everything. Feed it isotonic-calibrated scores from
*the same model* and it flags 3,345.

Across the seven cost ratios we measured, the formula on raw scores overspends
by 8% to 56%; on calibrated scores, by 1% to 7%. The diagnostic is a
reliability plot, not a code review — the bug is in the numbers, not the
arithmetic.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-classification-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On attribution — the same caution as @sec-text-as-data.** These are questions
that recur across the two credible public sources, both free:
[*Introduction to Machine Learning Interviews*](https://huyenchip.com/ml-interviews-book/)
by Chip Huyen [@huyen2021interviews] and
[Machine Learning Interviews](https://github.com/alirezadir/Machine-Learning-Interviews).
Treat any page claiming to list "the questions company X asks" as marketing.
:::

1. **How do you handle class imbalance?** The expected answer lists oversampling,
   undersampling, SMOTE and class weights. The better answer starts by asking
   what breaks, because the answer is usually the *threshold*, not the model.
   Give the measurement: on a 6.32% minority class, moving one threshold reached
   77.66 macro-F1 against 76.09 for class weights, 77.63 for oversampling, 74.72
   for SMOTE and 62.98 for undersampling — with no refit and no extra rows. Then
   give the caveat, because it is the part that shows you understand the design:
   only the threshold arm was tuned, and average precision says a tuned
   oversampling arm would probably edge ahead. The finding is that the threshold
   is *free*, not that it is best. Then note that SMOTE was
   evaluated on nine low-dimensional dense numeric datasets and that its authors
   listed text as future work [@chawla2002smote] — that is the sentence that
   shows you read the paper rather than the blog post about it.

2. **Precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC — when do you use which?** Say what
   each divides by. FPR divides by the majority count; precision divides by what
   you flagged. On an imbalanced problem those denominators differ by orders of
   magnitude, so the two curves rank models differently
   [@davis2006relationship] — ours disagreed in direction between two BERTurk
   checkpoints. Finish with the practical rule: quote PR-AUC against the base
   rate so the reader can see the lift, and never quote accuracy without the
   majority-class rate beside it.

3. **What is calibration, and how would you test it?** A model is calibrated when
   among the cases it scores 0.8, about 80% really are positive. Test it with a
   reliability diagram and an expected calibration error, and then — this is the
   part most candidates miss — say *which* ECE. Guo et al.'s version bins the top-label
   confidence $\max_k p_k$ and asks how often the `argmax` is right
   [@guo2017calibration]; binning on $P(\text{class }1)$ is a different statistic.
   On our class-weighted model they read 8.98 and 14.18. Both are correct; a
   number without its definition is not.

4. **Platt scaling or isotonic regression?** Isotonic is non-parametric and can
   fit any monotone distortion; Platt is a two-parameter sigmoid and cannot
   [@platt1999probabilistic; @zadrozny2002transforming]. The decision is about
   how much held-out data you have: Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana found Platt ahead
   below roughly 200–1,000 calibration points and isotonic level or better above
   that [@niculescu2005predicting]. Name the size of your calibration set. Ours
   is 8,000, and isotonic came out at 0.69 against Platt's 0.94 — a gap inside
   our own estimator's noise, so what we can say is that **both are adequate at
   this calibration-set size**, which is what their result predicts. Saying
   "isotonic won" would be reading a quarter of a point off a statistic whose
   floor is half a point.

5. **How would you pick the decision threshold for a production classifier?**
   Never 0.5 by default. Get a cost ratio from whoever owns the consequences,
   derive $q^*$ from it, and — the step that decides whether this works — verify
   the scores are calibrated before you trust the derivation. If the costs are
   fixed and you only need one operating point, sweeping the threshold directly
   on held-out data is a legitimate shortcut; in our measurements its regret
   stayed within two percentage points of the calibrate-then-derive route. Calibration earns its keep
   when the costs might change or the number gets shown to a person.

6. **When would you *not* use an LLM for classification?** When you have labels,
   when you have volume, and when you need a number rather than a word. Give the
   curve, not a verdict: on our task a prompted 36B mixture-of-experts beat a
   fine-tuned BERTurk by **8.79 macro-F1 at 1,000 labels**, tied it to **0.08
   points at 2,000** ($p = 0.97$), and lost by **4.73 at 40,000** — all paired-
   bootstrapped on the same 2,000 documents. Then price the tie: the encoder
   classifies a document **142× cheaper**, so a dead heat on quality is not a
   dead heat. Say which arrangement that number belongs to: a batched encoder
   against a single-stream 4-bit local server, which is the comparison a small
   team actually faces. A properly batched hosted API narrows the gap without
   changing the per-token arithmetic underneath. The part most candidates miss
   is the third axis. A zero-shot model
   returns the *word* `ŞİKAYET`, so you give up the ROC curve, the calibration
   map, the cost-derived threshold and the sweep — every instrument in this
   chapter. Our best prompted run sat at 56.98% precision and 80.95% recall and
   there was nothing to turn. Close by naming the literature and its limits:
   @edwards2024incontext found fine-tuning ahead by 0.119 micro-F1 with full data
   across 16 datasets but prompting ahead in the one-shot regime, and
   @bucher2024finetuned put the crossover above roughly 200 observations,
   measured against zero-shot BART-large-MNLI rather than a modern
   instruction-tuned model. Ours is an order of magnitude higher than theirs,
   which is the point — the crossover is a property of the pair you are
   comparing, not a constant.

7. **Your model is 94% accurate offline and users say it misses everything.
   Debug it.** Almost always the threshold, the base rate, or a distribution
   shift, in that order of likelihood. Check the confusion matrix, not the
   scalar: ours at 94.28% accuracy was catching 69 of 632 complaints. Then check
   whether the offline base rate matches production — a model calibrated on 6.32%
   complaints will systematically under-flag on a stream that runs at 15%. Then
   check for leakage into the offline number, and specifically whether any
   threshold or calibrator was fitted on the evaluation set.

### What carries over to more than two classes

Everything in this chapter is binary, and that is a choice rather than an
oversight: imbalance, thresholds and costs are clearest with one cut. Say which
parts move.

Three things carry over unchanged: **macro-F1**, the **majority-class floor**,
and reading your errors sorted by confidence. Two change shape. Single-label
multi-class has no per-class threshold to tune — the classes compete, so under
equal error costs the decision is an **argmax** over calibrated probabilities,
and Elkan's formula becomes an argmin over a full $K \times K$ cost matrix,
$\hat{y} = \arg\min_i \sum_j p_j C_{ij}$. Per-class thresholds belong to the
multi-label case below, where the classes do not compete. One threshold does
survive into multi-class, and it is worth building in: a *rejection* threshold on
$\max_k p_k$ or on the margin between the top two, sending anything below it to a
human instead of to a label. Calibration changes most: Platt and
isotonic are binary maps, so multi-class needs either one-vs-rest calibration or
a matrix- or vector-scaling variant — and this is the setting where the
top-label ECE of @guo2017calibration finally becomes the natural statistic
rather than a simplification. Multi-label is a third case again: $K$ independent
binary problems with $K$ independent thresholds, and a macro-F1 averaged over
labels whose base rates may differ by two orders of magnitude.

## The 2026 toolbox {#sec-classification-tools}

Everything in this chapter ran on one laptop with the versions below. Pinning
versions in a book is a hostage to fortune, but not pinning them is worse — the
numbers here are only reproducible against a stated stack.

| library | version used | what it is for here |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `scikit-learn` | 1.9.0 | `TfidfVectorizer`, `LogisticRegression`, `IsotonicRegression`, every metric and curve |
| `transformers` | 5.15.0 | loading and fine-tuning BERTurk |
| `torch` | 2.13.0 | the MPS backend the fine-tuning ran on |
| `imbalanced-learn` | 0.14.2 | `RandomOverSampler`, `RandomUnderSampler`, `SMOTE` |
| `scipy` | 1.18.0 | the bounded scalar minimiser that fits the temperature |
| `numpy` / `pandas` | 2.5.2 / 3.0.5 | array work, Parquet round-trip, the split |
| `ollama` | 0.24.0 | serving the four local LLMs in @sec-classification-llm — `llama3.2:3b`, `qwen3.5:9b`, `gemma3:27b`, `qwen3.6:35b-a3b`, all `Q4_K_M` quantised |

: The stack these numbers came from. Python 3.14.5, Apple Silicon
{tbl-colwidths="[26,16,58]"}

Worth knowing about, not used above:

| library | current version | when you would reach for it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `setfit` | 1.1.3 | the contrastive few-shot recipe of @tunstall2022setfit as one object. The right first try when you have tens of labels per class rather than hundreds |
| ModernBERT and its multilingual descendants | 2025–2026 | the encoders to try *before* BERTurk on a new project [@warner2025modernbert] — same fine-tuning recipe, rotary embeddings, an 8,192-token context and markedly faster training |
| `sentence-transformers` | 5.7.0 | frozen embeddings plus a linear head — often within a point or two of full fine-tuning at a fraction of the training cost |
| `peft` / `accelerate` | 0.20.0 / 1.14.0 | LoRA and distributed training when the encoder no longer fits the way it did here (@sec-post-training) |
| `netcal` | 1.4.0 | calibration methods and diagrams beyond what `scikit-learn` ships, including binning and beta calibration |
| `mapie` | 1.5.0 | conformal prediction — instead of a calibrated probability, a *set* of labels with a guaranteed coverage rate. The right tool when "I don't know" must be a valid output |
| `cleanlab` | 2.9.0 | finds label errors in your training data. On a corpus whose labels came from star ratings, this is usually the highest-return hour you can spend |
| `optuna` | 4.9.0 | hyper-parameter search when the sweep stops fitting in a `for` loop |
| `onnxruntime` | 1.28.0 | exporting a fine-tuned encoder for CPU serving, typically 2–4× faster than PyTorch eager mode at inference |
| `skops` | 0.14.0 | persisting `scikit-learn` models without `pickle`, which you should not be deserialising from anywhere you do not control |
| `shap` | 0.52.0 | per-prediction attributions when somebody asks *why* — see @sec-classification-errors for the cheaper alternative |

: The wider ecosystem, versions as of writing {tbl-colwidths="[18,14,68]"}

::: {.column-margin}
Two omissions are deliberate. `xgboost` (3.4.1) and `lightgbm` (4.7.0) are
excellent on tabular data and rarely competitive on high-dimensional sparse text,
where a linear model with an L2 penalty is already close to the right inductive
bias. And `fasttext` (0.9.3) remains a genuinely fast supervised baseline, but it
is effectively unmaintained; `scikit-learn` gets you to the same place on a
corpus this size.
:::

## Lab: ship a classifier with a real serving budget {#sec-classification-lab}

The deliverable is one paragraph of the form *"we flag X% of incoming documents,
catch Y% of the Z, at a cost of W milliseconds per document — and here is the
threshold we chose and why"*. Every clause has to be defensible from a
measurement you made.

### What you need

A corpus of a few thousand documents with a binary label you did not create by
hand — star ratings, resolved/unresolved tickets, spam flags, moderation
outcomes. It must be **imbalanced**; if your minority class is over 30%, subsample
it until it is not, because the whole discipline of this chapter only matters when
the classes are lopsided. `scikit-learn` alone is enough for steps 1 through 5.

### Step 1 — write down the floor before you train anything

Report the majority-class rate, and the accuracy and macro-F1 of three trivial
policies: all-majority, all-minority, and a coin flip. This takes four lines and
it is the single most useful table in your report, because every later number
gets read against it. Ours were 93.68 / 6.32 / 50.21 accuracy, and 48.37 / 5.94 /
38.57 macro-F1.

### Step 2 — split three ways, not two

`fit`, `cal`, `test` — 64 / 16 / 20 is a reasonable default and is what this
chapter used. Write down, before you continue, which quantities are allowed to
touch `cal`: the threshold, the calibrator, the cost-optimal operating point.
Nothing may touch `test` until step 7.

If you cannot spare a calibration slice, say so explicitly and use
cross-validated calibration instead — but do not quietly fit the calibrator on
training data. The measured penalty for doing that here was ECE 2.39 against 0.69,
and the reason it is dangerous is that 2.39 does not look wrong.

### Step 3 — build the sparse baseline and the label-budget curve

tf-idf over 1–2 grams into logistic regression. Then refit at 200, 500, 1,000,
2,000 and all of your labels, and plot macro-F1 against budget. You are looking
for two things: whether the curve has flattened (ours had not, even at 40,000),
and how much of the gain is in the minority class (ours: 20.75 points of macro-F1
against 41.84 of minority F1).

### Step 4 — sweep the threshold on `cal` and report the table

For $t$ from 0.05 to 0.95, record accuracy, precision, recall, minority F1,
macro-F1 and MCC. Two questions to answer from the table: how much did accuracy
move over the range $t \ge 0.2$, and is the highest-accuracy threshold the same
as the highest-macro-F1 one? On this corpus (read on `test`, for illustration)
the answers were *1.3 points* and
*no*. (Sweep below 0.2 as well and accuracy collapses to 68.98 — which is why
the interesting range is the one where accuracy looks flat.)

### Step 5 — check whether your scores are probabilities

Bin the predicted scores, plot observed frequency against mean predicted
probability, and compute ECE and MCE. State which ECE you computed. Then fit
Platt and isotonic on `cal` and re-measure. If your ECE is already under about 1
you can stop; if it is over 5, anything downstream that treats the score as a
probability is wrong by a margin you can now quantify.

### Step 6 — turn a cost into a threshold

Ask someone who owns the consequences for a ratio $r = C_{FN}/C_{FP}$. Do not
accept "they're both bad"; make them choose a number, even a rough one, because
the alternative is that the number gets chosen by whoever wrote 0.5. Compute
$q^* = 1/(1+r)$, apply it to your calibrated scores, and report total cost
against the two trivial policies. If your model cannot beat *flag everything*,
that is a publishable finding about your project.

### Step 7 — open `test` once

Run every chosen threshold and calibrator, produce the confusion matrix, and
write the paragraph. Then run one more thing: **time it**. Documents per second,
single process, at the batch size you would actually serve. A model you cannot
afford to run is not a model, and this is the number people forget to measure
until the week they deploy.

### What to hand in

The trivial-baseline table, the label-budget curve, the threshold sweep, the
reliability plot before and after calibration, the cost table, and the paragraph.
Roughly two pages. If any number in the paragraph does not appear in one of the
tables, delete the number.

## Exercises {#sec-classification-exercises}

1. **Reproduce the floor.** On any imbalanced corpus you have, compute the
   accuracy of a classifier that always predicts the majority class. Then find a
   published result on that corpus and check how far above the floor it sits.
   Report both numbers together.

2. **Break a threshold.** Take a trained binary classifier and sweep its
   threshold from 0.05 to 0.95. Plot accuracy and minority-class recall on the
   same axes. Report the threshold that maximises accuracy and the threshold that
   maximises macro-F1, and explain in one sentence why they differ.

3. **Prove the ranking did not move.** Repeat the experiment in
   @sec-classification-imbalance on your own data: compare "no correction plus a
   tuned threshold" against `class_weight="balanced"`. Report macro-F1 *and*
   average precision for both. Explain what it would mean if the average
   precisions were equal, and what it would mean if they were not.

4. **Cost the mistakes.** Build a cost matrix for a task where a false negative
   costs 10× a false positive. Derive $q^*$, apply it to raw and to calibrated
   scores, and report the total cost of each against the cost of flagging
   everything. State how much calibration was worth in your units.

5. **Break the calibrator on purpose.** Fit an isotonic calibrator on your
   *training* scores instead of held-out ones, and measure ECE both ways. The
   point of the exercise is to see how unremarkable the leaked number looks.

6. **Find the crossover.** Fine-tune an encoder at 200, 500, 1,000 and 2,000
   labels and plot it against your sparse baseline on the same axes. Report the
   budget at which the curves cross, and the wall-clock cost of each point.
   Compare with our crossover and account for any difference — corpus size,
   language, document length, or class balance.

7. **Read fifty errors.** Sample fifty documents your best model got wrong,
   stratified by confidence, and label the failure mode of each by hand. Report
   the three most common modes with counts. If the largest category is
   "the label is wrong", you have learned something more valuable than any
   architecture change.

8. **Re-measure the folklore.** Take one local model and run zero-shot
   classification on 500 documents twice: once with the instruction in your
   corpus's language, once in English. Report the difference with a *paired*
   bootstrap over the same documents, not two separate intervals. Then repeat
   with a model at least 3× larger. State whether the advice "write prompts in
   English" survives on either.

9. **Check the parse rate before you check the score.** Instrument a zero-shot
   run to record, per document, the raw response, the finish reason, and whether
   your parser succeeded. Now cap the output at 8 tokens and re-run. Report the
   accuracy *and* the parse rate, and say what the accuracy would have looked
   like if you had logged only the accuracy. Use a model that has a reasoning or
   thinking mode — the failure needs one, which is itself the lesson.

10. **Price the tie.** Suppose a prompted model and a fine-tuned one score
    within noise of each other on your task. Measure seconds per 1,000 documents
    for both, at the batch size you would actually serve. Compute the volume at
    which the fine-tune's one-off training cost is repaid, and the monthly bill
    for each at your real traffic. Then say which you would ship and why —
    the answer is allowed to be the slower one. State whether your repayment
    volume counts the cost of *producing* the labels. If it does not, say so in
    the same sentence as the number.

## Where to go deeper {#sec-classification-deeper}

One thing first: plot your classifier's predicted probabilities as a
histogram. If they pile up at 0 and 1, that is a reason to check calibration
against observed frequencies rather than a verdict on its own — a genuinely
easy problem produces confident probabilities that are also correct. Make the
reliability diagram, and if the confidence is not earned,
@sec-classification-calibration is the section you need rather than a bigger
encoder.

| [Hugging Face LLM course](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course) | the fine-tuning chapters, if you want the encoder path spelled out end to end |
| [`setfit`](https://github.com/huggingface/setfit) | few-shot classification without a prompt, and the baseline to beat before you reach for an LLM |
| [Chip Huyen's blog](https://huyenchip.com/blog/) | the applied-ML framing of when a classifier is the right product decision at all |
| [StatQuest](https://www.youtube.com/%40statquest) — Josh Starmer | the reference channel for the statistics under this chapter — ROC, precision-recall, and calibration explained slowly and correctly |

## What to remember {#sec-classification-summary}

- **Compute the floor before you compute anything else.** This corpus is 93.68%
  satisfied, so a model with no features, no parameters and no training scores
  **93.68% accuracy and 48.37 macro-F1**. Every accuracy figure in a classification
  paper should be read as a distance from that number, and on imbalanced data
  the distance is usually small enough to be embarrassing.
- **A threshold is a free 19 points.** The identical fitted model — the same
  coefficients, byte for byte — goes from **58.24 to 77.66 macro-F1** because we
  flagged at 0.166 instead of 0.5. Average precision stayed at
  60.30 and AUC at 93.24 through the change, which is the proof that nothing
  about the model moved.
- **Try the threshold before you touch the data.** Across five imbalance
  treatments, moving the cut reached 77.66 against oversampling's 77.63, class
  weighting's 76.09 and SMOTE's 74.72 — at zero training cost, and with only the
  threshold arm tuned, so read it as *the same operating point for free* rather
  than as a win. Undersampling actively destroyed the model (62.98, average precision down from 60.30 to 52.49
  because 87.4% of the training rows were thrown away). @elkan2001foundations,
  who is routinely cited *in support of* rebalancing, argues the opposite: learn
  from the data as given, then compute the decision.
- **Resampling is not free even when it works.** @vandengoorbergh2022harm found
  that imbalance corrections damage calibration while doing little for
  discrimination, and we reproduced it on text: class weighting took ECE from
  **3.96 to 14.18** while gaining nothing a threshold could not have given.
- **The number your classifier prints is not a probability until you check.**
  Fit the calibrator on data the model has never seen. With 8,000 held-out
  documents isotonic regression and Platt scaling came out level (ECE **0.69**
  against 0.94 — a gap inside the noise floor computed above), which is what
  @niculescu2005predicting predicts above roughly 1,000 calibration points:
  there, isotonic is safe. Below that, Platt scaling is the safer choice. Fitting isotonic on
  the training scores instead gave 2.39: worse, but not obviously wrong, which
  is precisely what makes the mistake dangerous.
- **There are two ECEs and they are not comparable.** @guo2017calibration bin on
  top-label confidence $\max_k p_k$, which in a binary problem lives in
  $[0.5, 1]$; binning on $P(\text{class }1)$ is a different statistic. Say which
  one you computed.
- **A cost matrix picks the threshold for you.** $q^* = C_{FP} / (C_{FN} +
  C_{FP})$. Sweeping directly for the cost-minimising cut on held-out data did
  about as well as calibrating and applying the formula (1–6% regret against
  1–7%), so if you need one operating point for one fixed cost ratio you can
  skip calibration. Calibrate when the costs might change, when a person reads
  the number, or when something downstream multiplies it.
- **The encoder crossover is abrupt and it is early.** BERTurk loses to tf-idf
  at 200 and 500 labels, crosses between **500 and 1,000**, and by 2,000 labels
  scores 79.61 — beating tf-idf trained on the full **40,000** (76.21). Twenty
  times fewer labels for a better model. At equal budget the gap is 8.81
  macro-F1 and 15.45 complaint-F1.
- **Price that gap honestly.** The encoder costs roughly **970× more to train**
  for those 8.81 points (1,162 GPU-seconds against the vectoriser's 1.2), and
  serves about 470 documents per second against the vectoriser's tens of
  thousands. Whether that is
  worth it is a budget question, not a modelling one, and you cannot answer it
  without both numbers.
- **The prompted-versus-trained crossover is a curve, and on this task it sits
  at ~2,000 labels.** At 1,000 labels the prompted model wins by 8.79 macro-F1
  points (and by more below that); at 2,000 the two are a dead heat (0.08 points, $p = 0.97$); at 40,000
  the encoder wins by 4.73. Measure it on your own pair rather than citing
  anyone's number, because the crossover is a property of *which two models* you
  put on the axis.
- **Compare two models with a paired test, not by eyeballing two intervals.**
  Models scored on the same documents share most of their sampling noise, so
  overlapping marginal intervals prove nothing. Every comparison above is 10,000
  paired bootstrap resamples of the *difference*.
- **LLM folklore is true for weak models and small at best for strong ones.** Writing
  the instruction in English was worth **+16.90** macro-F1 on a 3B model and
  **+0.54 (95% interval up to +2.25)** on a 9B one; eight examples were worth
  **+7.17** on `gemma3:27b` and **+0.51 (up to +2.48)** on `qwen3.6:35b-a3b`.
  Quote the intervals rather than the p-values: what the strong-model runs
  establish is a ceiling of two-and-a-half points, not a zero. Both rules were
  real once. Re-measure them on the model you are shipping.
- **Prompting costs you the threshold.** Every prompted run here was
  recall-biased on the minority class — the best reached 56.98% precision at
  80.95% recall against BERTurk's 74.42/76.19 — and none of it is fixable,
  because a zero-shot model returns a *word*. No ROC, no isotonic map, no $q^*$,
  no sweep. That is a larger loss than the macro-F1 gap.
- **A stated confidence can be right on average and still separate nothing.**
  `qwen3.5:9b` averaged 93.53% stated against 92.95% actual — a +0.58 gap, and
  an ECE of 1.80 over its nine self-chosen bins — while putting **1,549 of the
  2,000 documents on the single value 95**. As an error detector it scores AUROC 0.667
  against the encoder's own 0.843, and the ≥95 routing cut that looks useful was
  read off the evaluation set, so treat it as an oracle until you re-pick it on
  held-out data.
- **The ensemble opportunity is real and usually unaffordable.** The best LLM
  and BERTurk disagree on 94 of 2,000 documents, and an oracle picking the winner
  each time would gain 5.81 macro-F1 points. Collecting them means paying 142×
  more per document in the arrangement we measured. Cross-tabulate to find the opportunity; price it before you
  believe in it.
- **Replacing a model is a trade.** BERTurk fixes 332 test documents and breaks
  149 that tf-idf handled — a net 183, or 1.83 accuracy points. Build the
  disagreement 2×2 every time you swap a model, because the aggregate delta
  hides which documents you gave up.
- **The encoder's advantage is concentrated where you would expect.** tf-idf's
  error rate is flat across document length (4.86%–5.82%, no trend); BERTurk's
  falls from 4.50% on the shortest reviews to 3.10% on 200–399 characters. It is
  not uniformly better — it is better at long documents, because that is where
  negation, concession and scope live.
- **Sort your errors by confidence, not at random.** The top of that list is
  where label errors concentrate. Ours includes a review that says the product
  broke in two months *and explains that it is giving five stars so the
  complaint appears at the top of the listing* — labelled satisfied, because our
  labels come from star ratings. When the model looks more right than the label,
  stop tuning and go re-read @sec-audit; @frenay2014classification is the survey.
- **Some of your test set is unlabelable.** 204 documents defeat both models and
  137 of them are complaints — 21.7% of every complaint in the test set. One of
  them is a review whose entire text is the word "downside" followed by a colon.
  No architecture reaches those, and their existence caps the score you can
  honestly chase.
- **Suspect your harness before your model — especially when the number is
  good.** In our timing sweep one inference run came back 27× slower than the
  other seven and one training epoch was 14× slower than its two siblings.
  Neither was a property of the model. But the expensive failure ran the other
  way: an LLM scored 93.75% accuracy and 48.39 macro-F1, which *is* the
  majority-class baseline, because a reasoning model spent its 24-token budget
  inside a `thinking` field the parser never read, and every unparseable answer
  fell through to the majority label. A bad number gets investigated; a good one
  gets published. Design against that asymmetry — never impute a label on a parse
  failure, abort on a low parse rate, smoke-test before the overnight queue —
  because your own scepticism will not fire when the result is what you hoped
  for.
